studyMetadata.title: Introducing Acts
studyMetadata.subtitle: An eight-session overview of the book of Acts
studyMetadata.description: A first look at the book of Acts for individuals and small groups. Eight key passages, with summaries of what lies between, trace the good news about Jesus from Jerusalem to Rome.
studyMetadata.author: Rick Creighton

elements.text:
Welcome to Introducing Acts. This study is for anyone coming to the book of Acts for the first time, or coming back to it after a long gap. Over eight sessions we will work through eight key passages that together give a feel for the whole book: how the good news about Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome.

Each session follows the same pattern. You will find a short summary of the part of Acts we have skipped since the previous session, and then a main passage to study. Tap the verse reference on a question to read the passage in a pop-up. Write your own answer, then tap Check [[icon:localValidate]] to see how it compares with the passage. At the end of each session, Read more takes you to a Go Deeper section with extra background, or a fuller account of the chapters we skipped.

You can use this study on your own or in a group. On your own, go at your own pace. In a group, each member works through the session beforehand, and the group then meets to share answers and talk about the reflection questions. If you are leading a group, you can switch on the Leaders’ Notes in Settings.

elements.question: What do you already know about the book of Acts, and what would you like to find out?

elements.text:
Acts is Luke’s second volume. His first is the Gospel that bears his name, and Acts tells what happened after Jesus returned to the Father. The book follows the outline Jesus gives in 1:8: the news spreads from Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), through Judea and Samaria (8–12), and on towards the farthest parts of the earth (13–28), ending in Rome.

We cannot read all twenty-eight chapters in eight sessions, so we will pause at eight key moments and fill in the gaps with short summaries. Along the way you will meet the coming of the Spirit, the first church under pressure, the conversion of Saul, the door opening to the Gentiles, the church’s decision about grace, the gospel in one of the world’s great cities, and Paul’s final witness in Rome. We begin where Luke begins his story: with Jesus’ last words and his departure.

elements.passageText:
1I wrote the former account, Theophilus, about all that Jesus began to do and teach 2until the day he was taken up to heaven, after he had given orders by the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. 3To the same apostles also, after his suffering, he presented himself alive with many convincing proofs. He was seen by them over a forty-day period and spoke about matters concerning the kingdom of God. 4While he was with them, he declared, “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait there for what my Father promised, which you heard about from me. 5For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

6So when they had gathered together, they began to ask him, “Lord, is this the time when you are restoring the kingdom to Israel?” 7He told them, “You are not permitted to know the times or periods that the Father has set by his own authority. 8But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the farthest parts of the earth.”

9After he had said this, while they were watching, he was lifted up and a cloud hid him from their sight. 10As they were still staring into the sky while he was going, suddenly two men in white clothing stood near them 11and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking up into the sky? This same Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come back in the same way you saw him go into heaven.”

elements.question: In verse 1, Luke looks back on his first account. What does he say it was about, and what might the word ‘began’ suggest about what comes next?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the word ‘began’ in verse 1.
elements.questionHint:
Ask what Jesus ‘began’ to do and teach in Luke’s first book.
Ask what that word suggests about whether his work has ended.
Look at who carries on the work in verses 2–8.
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke says his first book dealt with everything Jesus started doing and teaching before he was taken up. The word ‘began’ hints that the story is not finished at the ascension. Acts goes on to show the risen Jesus continuing that same ministry through the apostles, by the Holy Spirit.
elements.mainPoint: Acts continues what **Jesus began**: the risen Lord goes on working through his apostles by the Spirit.

elements.question: What evidence does Luke give in verses 2–3 that Jesus was really alive after his suffering?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at what Luke says Jesus gave the apostles in verse 3.
elements.questionHint:
Find the phrase about proofs, and how long the apostles saw him.
Notice what Jesus spoke to them about during those days.
elements.sampleAnswer: After his death on the cross Jesus showed himself alive to the apostles, giving them many compelling evidences. For forty days they kept seeing him, so it was no fleeting vision. In those weeks he taught them about God’s kingdom.
elements.mainPoint: The resurrection was **real and well attested**: for forty days Jesus appeared alive to the apostles and taught about the kingdom.

elements.question: What does Jesus tell the apostles to do in verses 4–5, and what does he promise?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what they are told to do, and what they are told to wait for.
elements.questionHint:
Notice where they must stay.
Notice who has made the promise.
Compare John’s baptism with what is coming.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus instructs the apostles to stay in Jerusalem until the Father’s gift arrives. He contrasts John, who immersed people in water, with what is about to happen: within days they will be immersed in the Holy Spirit. The gift is promised by God, so they cannot manufacture it themselves.
elements.mainPoint: The Spirit is **the Father’s promised gift**: the apostles are to wait in Jerusalem for it, not produce it.

elements.question: What question do the apostles ask in verse 6, and how does Jesus respond in verse 7?
elements.questionHintFirst: Read the apostles’ question carefully, and then see how Jesus replies.
elements.questionHint:
Find the words ‘restoring’ and ‘Israel’ in the question.
In verse 7, notice what is not for them to know, and who sets the times.
elements.sampleAnswer: The apostles ask whether Jesus is about to restore Israel’s kingdom. He answers that the dates are not theirs to learn, because the Father has fixed them on his own authority. The matter of timing is God’s alone.
elements.mainPoint: The timing of the kingdom is **the Father’s alone**: the apostles are not given the dates, only a task.

elements.question: What will the apostles receive according to verse 8, and what will they do as a result?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what comes first, and what follows from it.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they will receive, and when.
Then find what they will be as a result.
elements.sampleAnswer: When the Holy Spirit arrives, the apostles will be given power. That power equips them to be Jesus’ witnesses. Their testimony will rest on the Spirit’s strength and not on their own.
elements.mainPoint: The Spirit gives **power for witness**: Jesus’ people testify about him because the Spirit has come on them.

elements.question: Verse 8 names several places. List them, and say what you notice about how far the mission reaches.
elements.questionHintFirst: Read the list of places as a map.
elements.questionHint:
Find the places named in verse 8, in order.
Notice how each is further from where the apostles are standing than the one before.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus names Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, and finally the farthest corners of the world. The mission starts in the city of the cross and spreads in widening rings. It reaches out first to neighbours, then to a mixed people, and at last beyond every border, well past the apostles’ own nation.
elements.mainPoint: The mission **widens in circles**, from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the farthest parts of the earth.

elements.question: What do the apostles see happen in verse 9, and how is it described?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice who watches, and what takes Jesus out of sight.
elements.questionHint:
Look at the verbs that describe what happens to Jesus.
Find what hides him from their sight.
elements.sampleAnswer: As the apostles looked on, Jesus rose into the air and a cloud took him from view. He was carried up to heaven openly, with witnesses present. Luke makes clear that they saw it with their own eyes.
elements.mainPoint: The ascension was **visible and public**: Jesus was lifted up to heaven in a cloud before the apostles’ eyes.

elements.question: What do the two men in white clothing say to the disciples in verses 10–11, and what do they promise?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice that the two men ask a question before they make a promise.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they ask the disciples.
Find what they say about ‘this same Jesus’.
Notice how they say he will return.
elements.sampleAnswer: Two men in white ask the disciples why they are standing there gazing at the sky. They promise that the very Jesus who has left will return, in the manner he departed. So the disciples should stop staring upward and get on with the task they were given, sure that he will come back.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus will **return in the same way** he left, so his people are to work with hope, not stand gazing.

elements.question: Jesus’ followers were told to wait for the Spirit rather than rush ahead. Where are you tempted to act in your own strength, and what would waiting on God look like there?
The mission begins in Jerusalem and moves outwards. Who are the ‘Jerusalem’, the ‘Judea and Samaria’ and the ‘farthest parts of the earth’ people in your own life?
Jesus promises that he will return. How does that hope shape the way you live this week?

elements.text: In this session we have seen Jesus hand on a mission: wait for the Spirit, then be his witnesses, starting where you are and reaching outwards. If you want to know more about who wrote Acts, why, and what the world of Acts was like, tap Read more below. Next time we go to the day the Spirit came, and hear the first sermon of the church.

chapters.chapterTitle: The first sermon and the first church

elements.text: The Spirit has come, and a crowd has gathered. In this session we listen to the first Christian sermon ever preached, and see what happens to those who hear it. As you work, notice how much of Peter’s message is about Jesus, and how the new community shapes its life.

elements.question: If you had to explain to a friend in two sentences who Jesus is, what would you say?

elements.text: After Jesus’ ascension the apostles return to Jerusalem and devote themselves to prayer, together with Jesus’ mother, his brothers and other followers. Peter leads the group to replace Judas, and Matthias is chosen to restore the number of the Twelve. Then, on the Day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes: there is a sound like a violent wind, what looks like tongues of fire rests on the believers, and they begin to speak in other languages. Pilgrims from across the Mediterranean world, gathered in Jerusalem for the festival, hear the wonders of God declared in their own languages. Some are amazed and others sneer. Peter stands up with the other eleven apostles and begins to explain, quoting the prophet Joel. Our passage picks up in the middle of Peter’s sermon.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 1:12–2:21 in your own Bible to see how the sermon begins. If you would like a fuller account of these verses, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
22“Men of Israel, listen to these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man clearly attested to you by God with powerful deeds, wonders, and miraculous signs that God performed among you through him, just as you yourselves know— 23this man, who was handed over by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you executed by nailing him to a cross at the hands of Gentiles. 24But God raised him up, having released him from the pains of death, because it was not possible for him to be held in its power.

25For David says about him, ‘I saw the Lord always in front of me, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken. 26Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; my body also will live in hope, 27because you will not leave my soul in Hades, nor permit your Holy One to experience decay. 28You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of joy with your presence.’

29“Brothers, I can speak confidently to you about our forefather David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. 30So then, because he was a prophet and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath to seat one of his descendants on his throne, 31David by foreseeing this spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was neither abandoned to Hades, nor did his body experience decay. 32This Jesus God raised up, and we are all witnesses of it.

33So then, exalted to the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out what you both see and hear. 34For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand 35until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ 36Therefore let all the house of Israel know beyond a doubt that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ.”

elements.question: How does Peter describe Jesus’ ministry in verse 22, and who does he say was behind Jesus’ death in verse 23?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice that Peter says two things about the death of Jesus.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God did through Jesus in verse 22.
In verse 23, find whose plan it was and who carried out the act.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter reminds the crowd that God had vouched for Jesus through miracles that they had witnessed themselves. Yet this same Jesus was delivered up according to God’s fixed purpose and advance knowledge, and they had him put to death by lawless men. Peter does not play down either side: the death was God’s plan, and the crowd bear the guilt of killing him.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus’ death was both **God’s plan and the crowd’s deed**: God vouched for him by miracles, yet they had him killed.

elements.question: What does God do in verse 24, and why could death not keep its hold?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice who is acting in verse 24.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God did, and what he released Jesus from.
Find what Peter says was ‘not possible’.
elements.sampleAnswer: God brought Jesus back to life and freed him from the agony of death. Peter says it was impossible for death to keep its grip on him. The resurrection is God’s own act, and it vindicates Jesus as the one the miracles pointed to.
elements.mainPoint: **God raised Jesus** to life, because it was impossible for death to hold him.

elements.question: Peter quotes David in verses 25–28. What does Peter argue about David in verses 29–31, and what conclusion does he draw in verse 32?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about where David is now.
elements.questionHint:
In verses 29–30, find what Peter says about David’s death and his tomb.
Find what David knew God had sworn about his descendants.
Then read the conclusion in verse 32.
elements.sampleAnswer: David died and was buried, and his grave is still known, so his words about escaping decay cannot simply describe himself. Being a prophet who knew God had promised him a descendant on his throne, David was foreseeing the Messiah’s resurrection. Peter therefore declares that God has raised this Jesus, and that the apostles are witnesses of it.
elements.mainPoint: David, a prophet who died and was buried, was looking ahead to **the resurrection of the Christ**, of which the apostles are witnesses.

elements.question: According to verses 33–36, where is Jesus now, what has he done, and what must Israel know?
elements.questionHintFirst: Follow what Jesus has done, step by step.
elements.questionHint:
Find where Jesus is in verse 33.
Find what he has done with the Spirit.
Find the two titles God has given him in verse 36.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus has been lifted to the place of honour at God’s right hand. From there he has sent out the Holy Spirit whom the Father promised, which explains what the crowd is witnessing. Israel is therefore to be completely certain that this crucified man has been made both Lord and Christ.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus reigns as Lord and Messiah**: raised to God’s right hand, he has sent out the Holy Spirit promised by the Father.

elements.passageText:
37Now when they heard this, they were acutely distressed and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “What should we do, brothers?” 38Peter said to them, “Repent, and each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” 40With many other words he testified and exhorted them saying, “Save yourselves from this perverse generation!” 41So those who accepted his message were baptized, and that day about 3,000 people were added.

42They were devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43Reverential awe came over everyone, and many wonders and miraculous signs came about by the apostles. 44All who believed were together and held everything in common, 45and they began selling their property and possessions and distributing the proceeds to everyone, as anyone had need. 46Every day they continued to gather together by common consent in the temple courts, breaking bread from house to house, sharing their food with glad and humble hearts, 47praising God and having the good will of all the people. And the Lord was adding to their number every day those who were being saved.

elements.question: How does the crowd respond in verse 37, and what does Peter tell them to do in verse 38?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the crowd’s question, and then Peter’s reply.
elements.questionHint:
Find how the crowd feels in verse 37.
Find Peter’s two commands in verse 38.
Find what Peter promises.
elements.sampleAnswer: The listeners are deeply shaken and ask the apostles what to do. Peter urges them to repent and to be immersed in the name of Jesus Christ, so that their sins are forgiven. He adds the promise that they will receive the Holy Spirit as a gift.
elements.mainPoint: Peter’s answer is **repent and be baptised**: forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit are promised to all who respond.

elements.question: Who is the promise for according to verse 39, and what happens that day (verses 40–41)?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how far Peter says the promise reaches.
elements.questionHint:
List the people the promise is for in verse 39.
Find what Peter urges in verse 40.
Find the result in verse 41.
elements.sampleAnswer: The promise reaches the crowd, their children and everyone far off, whoever the Lord our God summons. Peter pleads with them to rescue themselves from a crooked generation. Those who welcomed his word were baptised, and roughly 3,000 were added to the group that day.
elements.mainPoint: The promise reaches **everyone the Lord calls**, children and distant peoples alike, and about 3,000 respond that day.

elements.question: What four things were the believers devoting themselves to in verse 42?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for a list in verse 42.
elements.questionHint:
Find the four things the believers devoted themselves to.
Notice that they are all about shared life together.
elements.sampleAnswer: The new believers gave themselves wholeheartedly to four things. They listened to the apostles’ instruction, shared life as a family in fellowship, broke bread together and prayed. In short, the community was built on God’s word, one another, meals and prayer.
elements.mainPoint: A healthy church is built on **the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, shared meals and prayer**, the habits that hold believers together.

elements.question: How is the community’s life described in verses 43–45?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what people felt, and what people did.
elements.questionHint:
Find the word for how everyone felt.
Find what the apostles did.
Find what the believers did with their possessions.
elements.sampleAnswer: A sense of reverent awe settled on everyone, as the apostles performed many wonders. The believers stayed united and treated their belongings as common property. They sold land and goods and gave the money to whoever was in need.
elements.mainPoint: A generous community: **awe at God’s work and open hands** towards anyone in need, even to the point of selling property.

elements.question: What marked their daily life in verses 46–47, and what was the Lord doing?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about their daily rhythm: where, with whom, and how.
elements.questionHint:
Find where they met each day and where they ate.
Find how they felt as they ate and what they did.
Find what the Lord was adding.
elements.sampleAnswer: Day after day they gathered in the temple and ate in each other’s homes with cheerful, humble hearts. They went on praising God and enjoyed the favour of the whole city. And each day the Lord increased their number by adding those who were being rescued.
elements.mainPoint: The church lives **a glad, daily life of worship**, and the Lord keeps adding to it those who are being saved.

elements.question: The crowd asked, ‘What should we do?’ What would you say to a friend who asked you that question today?
Which of the four habits in verse 42 (teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer) is strongest in your life or your group, and which needs attention?
The early believers shared generously with those in need. Where might God be asking you to be more generous this week?

elements.text: Peter’s sermon centres on Jesus: crucified by human hands, raised by God, exalted to God’s right hand, and now Lord and Christ. The church that grows from it is devoted to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to bread and to prayer. To read a fuller account of the story leading up to Peter’s sermon, tap Read more. Next time we meet the church under pressure.

The good news is spreading quickly, and the authorities have noticed. In this session Peter and John are arrested, questioned and warned to keep quiet. Watch what they say to the rulers, and then what the whole church does when the two are released.

elements.question: Think of a time when you felt under pressure to keep quiet about something important to you. What made it hard?

elements.text: Soon after Pentecost, Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer. At the gate called Beautiful they meet a man who has been lame from birth and who is begging. Peter tells him, in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, to walk, and he leaps up and goes into the temple praising God. A crowd gathers in amazement at Solomon’s Portico, and Peter uses the moment to preach. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has glorified his servant Jesus, whom they handed over; God has raised him. Peter calls them to repent and turn to God so that their sins may be wiped out, and he reminds them that the prophets, from Moses onwards, foretold these things. Our passage begins while Peter and John are still speaking.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 3 in your own Bible to see how this episode starts. If you would like a fuller account, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
1While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests and the commander of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them, 2angry because they were teaching the people and announcing in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. 3So they seized them and put them in jail until the next day (for it was already evening). 4But many of those who had listened to the message believed, and the number of the men came to about 5,000.

5On the next day, their rulers, elders, and experts in the law came together in Jerusalem. 6Annas the high priest was there, and Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and others who were members of the high priest’s family. 7After making Peter and John stand in their midst, they began to inquire, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” 8Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, replied, “Rulers of the people and elders, 9if we are being examined today for a good deed done to a sick man—by what means this man was healed— 10let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healthy. 11This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, that has become the cornerstone. 12And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved.”

13When they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and discovered that they were uneducated and ordinary men, they were amazed and recognized these men had been with Jesus. 14And because they saw the man who had been healed standing with them, they had nothing to say against this.

15But when they had ordered them to go outside the council, they began to confer with one another, 16saying, “What should we do with these men? For it is plain to all who live in Jerusalem that a notable miraculous sign has come about through them, and we cannot deny it. 17But to keep this matter from spreading any further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.”

18And they called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. 19But Peter and John replied, “Whether it is right before God to obey you rather than God, you decide, 20for it is impossible for us not to speak about what we have seen and heard.” 21After threatening them further, they released them, for they could not find how to punish them on account of the people, because they were all praising God for what had happened. 22For the man, on whom this miraculous sign of healing had been performed, was over forty years old.

elements.question: Why were the authorities angry with Peter and John in verses 1–2, and what was the result of the apostles’ preaching in verses 3–4?
elements.questionHintFirst: Find the reason for the authorities’ anger in verse 2.
elements.questionHint:
Look at what Peter and John were teaching.
Find what the authorities did in verse 3.
Find the number at the end of verse 4.
elements.sampleAnswer: The priests, the temple captain and the Sadducees were furious that Peter and John were instructing the crowd and proclaiming the resurrection of the dead in Jesus. They arrested the two and locked them up overnight. Even so, many who heard the message trusted in Jesus, and the men numbered about 5,000.
elements.mainPoint: Peter and John are arrested for **proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus**, yet thousands of listeners still come to believe.

elements.question: What question are Peter and John asked in verse 7, and how does Peter answer in verses 8–10?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what the rulers ask, and whose name Peter gives.
elements.questionHint:
Find the two words the rulers use in verse 7.
Find what fills Peter in verse 8.
Find who Peter says healed the man.
elements.sampleAnswer: The rulers want to know what authority or name lay behind the healing. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, replies that the man is well through Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they put on a cross and whom God raised from the dead. He turns an inquiry about a kind deed into a witness to Jesus.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus’ name has power to heal**: the man is well because of Jesus of Nazareth, the one the rulers crucified and God raised.

elements.question: What two claims does Peter make about Jesus in verses 11–12?
elements.questionHintFirst: One claim uses an image from building, and the other is about salvation.
elements.questionHint:
Find what happened to the stone, and what it became.
Find the phrases ‘no one else’ and ‘no other name’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter applies the image of a discarded building block to Jesus: the builders threw him away, yet he has become the cornerstone. He adds that salvation is found in nobody else, since no other name has been given on earth through which people must be rescued. Jesus is both vindicated by God and the only way to be saved.
keyTerms: no one else|nobody else|no other name|only
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **God’s chosen cornerstone and the only Saviour**: there is no salvation in any other name.

elements.question: What surprised the council about Peter and John in verses 13–14, and what could they not deny?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what the council sees, and what they remember.
elements.questionHint:
Find how the rulers describe Peter and John.
Find what they recognise about them.
Find what they cannot argue against.
elements.sampleAnswer: The council noticed the confidence of Peter and John and realised they were untrained, common men, which amazed them. They concluded that these two had spent time with Jesus. And since the healed man was standing beside them, there was nothing they could say in reply.
elements.mainPoint: Their courage is explained by having been **with Jesus**, and the healed man standing there cannot be denied.

elements.question: What do the authorities order in verses 17–18, how do Peter and John answer in verses 19–20, and why do the authorities release them in verse 21?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare what the authorities command with what the apostles say.
elements.questionHint:
Find the order in verse 18.
Find the apostles’ reply in verses 19–20.
Find why the authorities let them go in verse 21.
elements.sampleAnswer: The authorities forbid them to speak or teach in Jesus’ name at all. Peter and John answer that the council itself must judge whether obeying men instead of God is right, for they cannot keep quiet about what they have seen and heard. After further warnings the rulers let them go, since the crowd was glorifying God and they could find no way to punish them.
keyTerms: not to speak|speak no more|not speak|forbid
elements.mainPoint: **God must be obeyed above any human authority**, so the apostles cannot stay silent about what they have seen and heard.

elements.passageText:
23When they were released, Peter and John went to their fellow believers and reported everything the high priests and the elders had said to them. 24When they heard this, they raised their voices to God with one mind and said, “Master of all, you who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and everything that is in them, 25who said by the Holy Spirit through your servant David our forefather, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot foolish things? 26The kings of the earth stood together, and the rulers assembled together, against the Lord and against his Christ.’

27“For indeed both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, assembled together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, 28to do as much as your power and your plan had decided beforehand would happen.

29And now, Lord, pay attention to their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your message with great courage, 30while you extend your hand to heal, and to bring about miraculous signs and wonders through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” 31When they had prayed, the place where they were assembled together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak the word of God courageously.

elements.question: When Peter and John are released, what do the believers do in verses 23–24, and how do they describe God?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how the believers begin their prayer.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they do when Peter and John are released.
Find how they address God.
Find what they say he has made.
elements.sampleAnswer: Once freed, Peter and John tell the others what the leaders threatened, and the whole company prays aloud together. They call God the sovereign Lord who created sky, land, sea and everything in them. Then they cite David, who by the Spirit spoke of the nations in uproar and rulers uniting against the Lord and his Anointed.
elements.mainPoint: The church prays to **the Creator of all things**, greater than the nations and rulers who rage against him.

elements.question: Who does the prayer say gathered against Jesus in verse 27, and what does verse 28 say about God’s plan?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the list of names, and then at who decided what would happen.
elements.questionHint:
List those who gathered against Jesus.
Find what they did to him.
Find whose plan decided it beforehand.
elements.sampleAnswer: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel’s people allied against Jesus, God’s holy servant whom he had anointed. Yet all they accomplished was what God’s hand and purpose had settled in advance. For the praying believers, even their enemies’ schemes lie within God’s control.
elements.mainPoint: God’s **sovereign plan** includes even the hostile acts of Herod, Pilate and the nations against his servant Jesus.

elements.question: What do the believers ask for in verses 29–30, and how does God answer in verse 31?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what the believers do not ask for.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they ask God to notice.
Find what they ask him to grant them.
Find how God answers in verse 31.
elements.sampleAnswer: The believers do not ask God to remove the danger. They ask him to take note of the threats and to enable them to declare his message fearlessly, while he heals and does signs. God answers by shaking the building and filling everyone with the Holy Spirit, and they go on to proclaim his word with courage.
elements.mainPoint: The church prays for **courage to speak**, not for safety, and God answers by filling them with his Spirit.

elements.question: The authorities tried to silence the apostles. What pressures today tempt Christians to stay quiet about Jesus?
The believers prayed for courage to keep speaking, not for the threats to stop. What do you tend to ask God for when you are under pressure?
The council recognised that Peter and John had been with Jesus. What would help others to see that about you?

elements.text: Peter and John refuse to stop speaking about Jesus, and the church responds to the threats by praying for courage. God answers by filling them with his Spirit, and they go on speaking his word boldly. To read a fuller account of the healing and sermon that led to this arrest, tap Read more. Next time we jump forward to one of the most surprising conversions in the New Testament.

Saul is one of the most determined opponents of the early church, and one of the least likely converts. In this session we see how Jesus meets him, how Ananias is drawn into the story, and how quickly the persecutor begins to preach.

elements.question: Who is the last person you would expect to become a Christian, and why?

elements.text: The chapters we skip show a church that is generous, tested and scattered. Believers share their possessions so that no one is in need, and Barnabas stands out for his gift. Ananias and Sapphira lie about their giving and are struck dead. The apostles are arrested again, freed by an angel, and defended before the council by the Pharisee Gamaliel. When Greek-speaking widows are overlooked, seven men, including Stephen and Philip, are appointed to serve. Stephen’s bold speech before the council ends in his death by stoning, with Saul looking on approvingly. A great persecution then scatters the church, and Philip takes the gospel to Samaria and meets an Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza. Our passage returns to Saul.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 7:54–8:3 in your own Bible, which tells of Stephen’s death and introduces Saul. If you want a fuller account of the chapters in between, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
1Meanwhile Saul, still breathing out threats to murder the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest 2and requested letters from him to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, either men or women, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

3As he was going along, approaching Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” 5So he said, “Who are you, Lord?” He replied, “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting! 6But stand up and enter the city and you will be told what you must do.”

7(Now the men who were traveling with him stood there speechless, because they heard the voice but saw no one.) 8So Saul got up from the ground, but although his eyes were open, he could see nothing. Leading him by the hand, his companions brought him into Damascus. 9For three days he could not see, and he neither ate nor drank anything.

elements.question: How does Luke describe Saul in verses 1–2, and what is he planning to do?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the unusual phrase ‘breathing out’.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Saul is breathing out.
Find what he asks the high priest for.
Find where he wants to bring those he arrests.
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul is still seething with menace and killing intent against the Lord’s followers. He obtains letters from the high priest for the synagogues in Damascus, so that he can seize anyone, man or woman, who follows the Way and drag them to Jerusalem in chains. He is a determined hunter of Christians.
elements.mainPoint: Saul is **a violent persecutor**, breathing threats and armed with letters to arrest believers in Damascus.

elements.question: What happens as Saul approaches Damascus in verses 3–4?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Saul sees and what he hears.
elements.questionHint:
Find what flashes around Saul.
Find what happens to him as a result.
Find the question the voice asks.
elements.sampleAnswer: As Saul nears Damascus, a blaze of light from the sky engulfs him. He collapses to the earth and hears a voice calling his name twice and asking why he is persecuting ‘me’. The question is aimed at him personally.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus **confronts Saul personally** in a flash of light, asking why he is persecuting him.

elements.question: Saul asks ‘Who are you, Lord?’ in verse 5. What does Jesus answer in verses 5–6, and what does he tell Saul to do?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how Jesus names himself, and what he says next.
elements.questionHint:
Find Saul’s question and Jesus’ answer.
Find who Jesus says Saul is persecuting.
Find what Jesus tells Saul to do.
elements.sampleAnswer: Saul asks who is speaking and addresses him as Lord. The answer is ‘I am Jesus, the one you are persecuting’. Jesus counts himself one with his people, so harming them is harming him; then he tells Saul to rise and enter the city, where instructions will be given.
keyTerms: told|what you must do|what he must do|instruct
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus identifies himself with his followers**, so to attack them is to attack him; Saul is told to rise and go into the city for instructions.

elements.question: What is Saul’s condition after the encounter in verses 7–9, and how do his companions react?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare the companions with Saul.
elements.questionHint:
Find what the companions heard and saw.
Find what Saul can and cannot do.
Find how long it lasts.
elements.sampleAnswer: His travelling companions are left dumbstruck: they heard a voice but could see nobody. Saul rises from the dust, yet though his eyes are open he is blind, so others take his hand and guide him into Damascus. For three days he cannot see, and he neither eats nor drinks.
elements.mainPoint: The encounter leaves Saul **helpless and blind**, led by the hand into Damascus for three days.

elements.passageText:
10Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias,” and he replied, “Here I am, Lord.” 11Then the Lord told him, “Get up and go to the street called ‘Straight,’ and at Judas’ house look for a man from Tarsus named Saul. For he is praying, 12and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and place his hands on him so that he may see again.”

13But Ananias replied, “Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, how much harm he has done to your saints in Jerusalem, 14and here he has authority from the chief priests to imprison all who call on your name!”

15But the Lord said to him, “Go, because this man is my chosen instrument to carry my name before Gentiles and kings and the people of Israel. 16For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

17So Ananias departed and entered the house, placed his hands on Saul and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you came here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, 19and after taking some food, his strength returned. For several days he was with the disciples in Damascus,

20and immediately he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “This man is the Son of God.” 21All who heard him were amazed and were saying, “Is this not the man who in Jerusalem was ravaging those who call on this name, and who had come here to bring them as prisoners to the chief priests?” 22But Saul became more and more capable, and was causing consternation among the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

elements.question: Why does Ananias hesitate when the Lord sends him to Saul in verses 10–14?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Ananias says he has heard.
elements.questionHint:
Find who has told him about Saul.
Find what Saul has done to the saints.
Find what authority Saul has in Damascus.
elements.sampleAnswer: Ananias objects because he has been told by many people how much damage Saul did to the Lord’s holy people in Jerusalem. He also knows Saul has been authorised by the chief priests to arrest all who call on the Lord’s name. His fear makes sense, yet he has already said ‘Here I am’ to the Lord.
elements.mainPoint: Ananias hesitates because he has **heard how much harm Saul has done** to God’s people, but he still obeys.

elements.question: What does the Lord say about Saul’s future in verses 15–16?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice that the Lord’s statement has two parts.
elements.questionHint:
Find the phrase ‘chosen instrument’.
Find who Saul will carry the Lord’s name before.
Find what Saul will suffer.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord tells Ananias that Saul is his selected tool to bear his name to the Gentiles, to kings and to Israel. He will also be shown how greatly Saul must suffer for that name. So Saul’s calling brings mission and hardship together.
elements.mainPoint: **God’s chosen instrument** to carry Jesus’ name to the nations, Saul is promised hardship along with his mission.

elements.question: What does Ananias say and do in verse 17, and what happens to Saul in verses 18–19?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Ananias calls Saul, and what happens to his eyes.
elements.questionHint:
Find how Ananias addresses Saul.
Find why the Lord Jesus sent him.
Find what happens after Saul can see again.
elements.sampleAnswer: Ananias lays his hands on Saul and greets him as ‘Brother’. He explains that the Lord Jesus sent him so that Saul would regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Something like flakes drops from Saul’s eyes, he sees, and he is baptised. Once he has eaten, his strength comes back.
elements.mainPoint: Saul is **welcomed as a brother**, healed, filled with the Spirit and baptised.

elements.question: What does Saul begin to do in verses 20–22, and how do people respond?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how quickly Saul begins.
elements.questionHint:
Find where he preaches and what title he gives Jesus.
Find how the hearers react in verse 21.
Find what Saul proves in verse 22.
elements.sampleAnswer: At once Saul starts announcing in the synagogues that Jesus is God’s Son. Everyone who heard him was astonished, since this was the man who had come to arrest Jesus’ followers. Saul grew steadily more powerful in argument and left the Damascus Jews bewildered by showing that Jesus is the Christ.
elements.mainPoint: The persecutor now **proclaims Jesus as the Son of God and the Christ**, to the amazement of the Damascus synagogues.

elements.question: Saul was sure that he was serving God, yet he was fighting against Jesus. Why might sincere people be wrong about Jesus, and is there any area where you might be resisting him?
Ananias obeyed even though he was afraid. When has God asked you to approach someone you were nervous about?
Who are you praying for who seems far from God? What does Saul’s story say about praying for them?

elements.text: Jesus stops a persecutor, names himself as the one Saul has been persecuting, and sends him to be his chosen instrument. Saul is changed, and the church’s greatest opponent becomes one of its greatest preachers. For a fuller account of the chapters between the church’s early years and Saul’s conversion, tap Read more. Next time we see the gospel cross another boundary.

Until now almost everyone who has believed in Jesus has been Jewish or Samaritan. In this session the gospel reaches a Roman household. Listen to what Peter says about Jesus, and then to what God does while he is still speaking.

elements.question: Is there a group of people you find it hard to imagine being welcome in your church? Why might that be?

elements.text: Saul begins to preach in Damascus, and when his life is threatened the disciples lower him over the city wall in a basket. In Jerusalem, Barnabas vouches for him, but he is soon sent away to Tarsus, and the church enjoys a period of peace. Peter, meanwhile, visits the coastal towns of Lydda and Joppa, where he heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha (also called Dorcas) from the dead. In Caesarea, Cornelius, a Roman centurion who fears God, is told by an angel to send for Peter. Before the messengers arrive, Peter has a vision of unclean animals and hears a voice telling him not to call unclean what God has made clean. He goes with the men and meets Cornelius and his household, who are gathered to hear what he has to say.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 10:1–33 in your own Bible to see how Peter and Cornelius come to meet. If you would like a fuller account of everything from Saul’s escape from Damascus onwards, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
34Then Peter started speaking: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism in dealing with people, 35but in every nation the person who fears him and does what is right is welcomed before him. 36You know the message he sent to the people of Israel, proclaiming the good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all)— 37you know what happened throughout Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John announced: 38with respect to Jesus from Nazareth, that God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. 39We are witnesses of all the things he did both in Judea and in Jerusalem. They killed him by hanging him on a tree, 40but God raised him up on the third day and caused him to be seen, 41not by all the people, but by us, the witnesses God had already chosen, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. 42He commanded us to preach to the people and to warn them that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. 43About him all the prophets testify, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

44While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the message. 45The circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were greatly astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles, 46for they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. Then Peter said, 47“No one can withhold the water for these people to be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did, can he?” 48So he gave orders to have them baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for several days.

elements.question: What has Peter just come to understand in verses 34–35, and what does it mean for people of every nation?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Peter says he now understands.
elements.questionHint:
Find the word ‘favouritism’.
Find who is welcomed in every nation.
Remember to read this alongside verse 43.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says he has come to see clearly that God treats no people group as favourites. Whoever in any nation reveres him and lives rightly is acceptable to him. This concerns God’s impartiality, not a way of earning his favour, and the divide between Jew and Gentile no longer decides who may come to God.
elements.mainPoint: God shows **no favouritism**: people from every nation are welcome to him, as the rest of Peter’s message makes plain.

elements.question: What message did God send, and who does Peter say is ‘Lord of all’ in verse 36?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the words in brackets in verse 36.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God sent, and to whom.
Find the title Peter gives Jesus in the brackets.
elements.sampleAnswer: God sent Israel the message of peace through Jesus Christ. Peter breaks in with a short aside that this Jesus Christ is Lord of everyone. Because he rules all people, the message cannot be limited to Israel.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus Christ is **Lord of all** and the one through whom God brings peace.

elements.question: How does Peter describe Jesus’ ministry in verses 37–38?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what anointed Jesus, and what he did.
elements.questionHint:
Find how Jesus was anointed.
Find two things he did.
Find the reason Peter gives.
elements.sampleAnswer: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power. He travelled about doing good and curing everyone oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. Peter presents Jesus’ ministry as God’s own power at work among people.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus’ ministry was **God’s power at work**, doing good and healing the oppressed, because God was with him.

elements.question: What does Peter say happened to Jesus in verses 39–41, and who saw him alive afterwards?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice who saw Jesus alive, and how they were chosen.
elements.questionHint:
Find how Jesus died.
Find what God did on the third day.
Find who saw Jesus, and what they did with him.
elements.sampleAnswer: They put Jesus to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and let him be seen. Not everyone saw him, only witnesses God had selected beforehand, who shared meals with him after his resurrection. That makes the apostles first-hand testifiers.
elements.mainPoint: The apostles are **chosen witnesses** who ate and drank with the risen Jesus.

elements.question: What has Jesus commanded the witnesses to do in verse 42, and what does Peter say the prophets promise in verse 43?
elements.questionHintFirst: One verse speaks of judgement, and the next of forgiveness.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Jesus commanded the witnesses to do.
Find what Jesus has been appointed as.
Find what the prophets say about everyone who believes.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus ordered the witnesses to proclaim to the people, and to testify that God has appointed him as judge over all, alive or dead. Peter adds that every prophet agrees: anyone who trusts in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Jesus is therefore both the judge and the source of pardon.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **judge of all and the only way to forgiveness** for everyone who believes in him.

elements.question: What happens while Peter is still speaking in verses 44–46, and how do the Jewish believers react?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what interrupts Peter, and who is astonished.
elements.questionHint:
Find what happens to those listening.
Find who is astonished, and why.
Find what the Gentiles are heard doing.
elements.sampleAnswer: While Peter is still talking, the Holy Spirit comes down on everyone listening. The Jewish believers who accompanied Peter are amazed that the gift has been given to Gentiles as well. Their proof is hearing the new believers speaking in tongues and magnifying God.
elements.mainPoint: God **pours out the Spirit** on Gentiles while Peter is still speaking, astonishing the Jewish believers.

elements.question: What question does Peter ask in verse 47, and what does he order in verse 48?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the reason Peter gives for baptism.
elements.questionHint:
Find Peter’s question about the water.
Find who has received the Spirit.
Find what he orders in verse 48.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter asks whether anyone can refuse the water of baptism to people who have received the Holy Spirit exactly as the Jewish believers did. He then commands that they be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ. So the Gentiles are received on equal terms, and they invite Peter to remain a few days.
elements.mainPoint: Gentiles who have received the Spirit are **welcomed by baptism** on exactly equal terms.

elements.question: Compare what Peter says in verses 34–35 with what God does in verses 44–48. How does the second confirm the first?
elements.questionHintFirst: Read verses 34–35 again, and then verses 44–48.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Peter says about God in verses 34–35.
Find what God does for the Gentiles in verses 44–46.
Ask how the second shows the first to be true.
elements.sampleAnswer: Early on Peter claims that God does not play favourites and that people of any nation are welcome. Then God proves it by giving the Holy Spirit to Gentiles exactly as he had to Jewish believers. Peter could not therefore deny baptism to people God had so plainly accepted.
elements.mainPoint: God’s action **confirms Peter’s claim**: having no favourites, he gives the Spirit to Gentiles exactly as he did to Jews.

elements.question: Peter had to unlearn a lifetime of assumptions about who was ‘in’. Which of your assumptions about other people might God be asking you to rethink?
In your church or group, who might feel like an outsider? What could you do to make them welcome?
Peter’s message centres on Jesus: his life, death, resurrection, judgement and forgiveness. How would you sum up the good news in a few sentences to a friend?

elements.text: Peter preaches Jesus as Lord of all, and God confirms it by giving the Spirit to Gentiles just as he had to Jewish believers. The church has to learn that the gospel is for every nation. To read more about the events that brought Peter to Cornelius’s house, tap Read more. Next time we see how the church handles the question this raises.

The gospel has crossed a boundary, and a question now has to be settled: do non-Jewish believers need to become Jewish to be saved? In this session the church meets to decide. Notice how the argument is settled, and what the church says about how people are saved.

elements.question: What is the hardest disagreement your church or group has had to deal with, and how was it handled?

elements.text: Back in Jerusalem, Peter is challenged for eating with Gentiles. He explains what happened, and the church praises God for granting repentance to life even to the Gentiles. Meanwhile, believers scattered by the persecution begin to preach to Greeks in Antioch, and a large number believe. Barnabas fetches Saul, and it is at Antioch that the disciples are first called Christians. Herod then kills James and imprisons Peter, but an angel frees him, and Herod dies. The Holy Spirit now sets apart Barnabas and Saul (who is now also called Paul), and the church at Antioch sends them out. They sail to Cyprus and then cross to the mainland, where Paul preaches in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch. Many Gentiles believe, but opposition forces them on. In Iconium, Lystra and Derbe the pattern repeats, and in Lystra Paul is stoned and left for dead. On the way back they strengthen the new churches and appoint elders.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 14:21–28 in your own Bible to see how the first journey ends. If you would like a fuller account of everything from chapter 11 onwards, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
1Now some men came down from Judea and began to teach the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” 2When Paul and Barnabas had a major argument and debate with them, the church appointed Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them to go up to meet with the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this point of disagreement. 3So they were sent on their way by the church, and as they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, they were relating at length the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers. 4When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were received by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all the things God had done with them. 5But some from the religious party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise the Gentiles and to order them to observe the law of Moses.”

6Both the apostles and the elders met together to deliberate about this matter. 7After there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that some time ago God chose me to preach to the Gentiles so they would hear the message of the gospel and believe. 8And God, who knows the heart, has testified to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, 9and he made no distinction between them and us, cleansing their hearts by faith. 10So now why are you putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to bear? 11On the contrary, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are.”

elements.question: What do the men from Judea teach in verse 1, and how do Paul and Barnabas respond in verse 2?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what the men say people need, and how the church decides to settle it.
elements.questionHint:
Find what the men from Judea teach.
Find how Paul and Barnabas react.
Find where the church sends them.
elements.sampleAnswer: Some men arrive from Judea insisting that unless the believers are circumcised in line with Moses’ practice, they cannot be saved. Paul and Barnabas strongly dispute this and a fierce debate follows. The church decides to send them with others to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders.
elements.mainPoint: The issue is **whether Gentiles must be circumcised in order to be saved**, and it is taken to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem.

elements.question: What news do Paul and Barnabas bring on the way and on arrival in verses 3–4, and what objection is raised in verse 5?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice joy first, and objection second.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Paul and Barnabas report along the way.
Find how the brothers react.
Find who raises the objection in verse 5.
elements.sampleAnswer: As they travel, Paul and Barnabas describe how Gentiles have turned to God, and the believers they meet are overjoyed. In Jerusalem they report what God had done through them. Then some believers who belonged to the Pharisees insist that Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep Moses’ law.
elements.mainPoint: Good news of Gentile conversion **meets a demand to add the law of Moses**, circumcision included.

elements.question: What does Peter remind the council about God’s dealings with the Gentiles in verses 7–9?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Peter points to as proof.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God chose Peter to do.
Find what God gave the Gentiles.
Find how God cleansed their hearts.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter recalls that God selected him to bring the message to non-Jews so they would hear and trust. God, who reads hearts, showed his acceptance by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did us. He drew no line between Jew and Gentile, since by faith he purified their hearts.
elements.mainPoint: God **accepts the Gentiles**, giving them the Spirit and cleansing their hearts by faith, exactly as he did for Jews.

elements.question: What does Peter warn against in verse 10, and what does he conclude about how people are saved in verse 11?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for a heavy word and a gracious word.
elements.questionHint:
Find the word ‘yoke’ and what Peter says about it.
Find what Peter says saves us.
Find who is saved in the same way.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter asks why they would test God by loading a burden on believers’ shoulders, a yoke that neither their forefathers nor they themselves could carry. He concludes that we trust we are saved through the Lord Jesus’ grace, exactly as the Gentiles are. Salvation is by grace for Jew and Gentile alike, not through taking on the law.
elements.mainPoint: **Salvation is by grace alone**: Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the Lord Jesus, and no burdensome law is added.

elements.passageText:
12The whole group kept quiet and listened to Barnabas and Paul while they explained all the miraculous signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.

13After they stopped speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. 14Simeon has explained how God first concerned himself to select from among the Gentiles a people for his name. 15The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written, 16‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and restore it, 17so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, namely, all the Gentiles I have called to be my own,’ says the Lord, who makes these things 18known from long ago.

19“Therefore I conclude that we should not cause extra difficulty for those among the Gentiles who are turning to God, 20but that we should write them a letter telling them to abstain from things defiled by idols and from sexual immorality and from what has been strangled and from blood. 21For Moses has had those who proclaim him in every town from ancient times, because he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

elements.question: What do Barnabas and Paul describe in verse 12, and how does the assembly respond?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the reaction of the assembly.
elements.questionHint:
Find what the whole group does.
Find who speaks, and what they describe.
elements.sampleAnswer: The whole assembly falls silent as Barnabas and Paul speak. They recount the miracles and wonders God performed among non-Jews through them. The gathering treats this as evidence of God’s own work among Gentiles.
elements.mainPoint: The council hears **what God has done among the Gentiles** through Paul and Barnabas, and falls silent.

elements.question: James refers to ‘Simeon’ in verse 14. What has Simeon explained about the Gentiles?
elements.questionHintFirst: Remember that ‘Simeon’ here is a form of Peter’s name.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Simeon has explained.
Find what God did first.
Find whom he took for his name.
elements.sampleAnswer: James refers to Simeon, that is Peter, who has described how God began by choosing from among the Gentiles a people to bear his name. The Gentile mission therefore starts with God’s own action. It is not the church’s invention.
elements.mainPoint: God himself **took the first step**, drawing a people for his name from among the Gentiles.

elements.question: What does James quote from the prophets in verses 15–18, and what does it promise?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice James’s appeal to the prophets.
elements.questionHint:
Find what James says about the prophets.
Find what God will rebuild.
Find who will seek the Lord as a result.
elements.sampleAnswer: James says the prophets agree with Peter and quotes a promise that God will rebuild David’s collapsed shelter. As a result everyone else, all the Gentiles called by God, will look for the Lord. Scripture itself therefore foresaw the Gentiles being included.
elements.mainPoint: The prophets **foretold the Gentiles’ inclusion**: God would rebuild David’s fallen tent so that the nations seek the Lord.

elements.question: What does James conclude in verses 19–21 about what should and should not be asked of Gentile believers?
elements.questionHintFirst: Contrast what James rules out with what he asks for.
elements.questionHint:
Find the phrase ‘extra difficulty’.
Find the four things he asks them to avoid.
Find the reason he gives in verse 21.
elements.sampleAnswer: James rules that Gentiles who are turning to God must not be weighed down with additional burdens. Instead they should be sent a letter telling them to keep away from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. He adds that Moses has long been preached in every city, with readings in the synagogues each Sabbath.
elements.mainPoint: **Nothing is added to grace**: no extra burden is laid on Gentiles beyond abstaining from idols, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood.

elements.question: The Jerusalem church could have insisted that Gentile believers adopt Jewish customs. Where might we be tempted to add requirements to the gospel today?
Peter says ‘we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus’. How easy do you find it to rest on grace rather than on your own record?
The church settled a serious disagreement by listening to testimony, turning to Scripture and reaching a decision. What can we learn from this about handling disagreement in our own church or group?

elements.text: The church decides that Gentiles are saved by grace, as Jews are, and not by taking on the law. This was one of the most important decisions in the history of the church, and it keeps the good news open to people from every background. To read a fuller account of the story from Peter’s defence to the end of the first journey, tap Read more. Next time we follow Paul to the city of Athens.

Paul has crossed into Europe, and in this session he finds himself alone in Athens, a city famous for its learning and crowded with idols. Watch what Paul does when the people he is speaking to know nothing about the Bible, and how he leads them towards Jesus.

elements.question: How would you explain who God is to someone who has never read the Bible or been to church?

elements.text: The Jerusalem council’s decision is carried to Antioch in a letter, and the church rejoices at its encouragement. Soon afterwards Paul and Barnabas disagree about taking John Mark and go separate ways. Paul chooses Silas, and Timothy joins them at Lystra. The Spirit steers them away from places they had planned to visit, and in a vision at Troas Paul sees a man from Macedonia asking for help. At Philippi a church begins in the home of Lydia, a seller of purple cloth. Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed after freeing a slave girl from a spirit, but an earthquake leads to the conversion of the jailer and his household. At Thessalonica a riot forces them out, and at Berea the Jews examine the Scriptures daily to check what Paul says. Hostile Jews from Thessalonica follow them, and Paul is sent on ahead to Athens.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 16:6–15 in your own Bible, which tells how the Spirit leads Paul to Macedonia. If you would like a fuller account of everything from the council’s letter onwards, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
16While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was greatly upset because he saw the city was full of idols. 17So he was addressing the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles in the synagogue, and in the marketplace every day those who happened to be there.

18Also some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers were conversing with him, and some were asking, “What does this foolish babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign gods.” (They said this because he was proclaiming the good news about Jesus and the resurrection.)

19So they took Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are proclaiming? 20For you are bringing some surprising things to our ears, so we want to know what they mean.” 21(All the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there used to spend their time in nothing else than telling or listening to something new.)

elements.question: How does Paul react to Athens in verse 16, and what does he do about it in verse 17?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice Paul’s feelings first, and then his actions.
elements.questionHint:
Find what upsets Paul about the city.
Find where he speaks.
Find who he speaks to in each place.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is deeply provoked to see Athens filled with idols. Instead of withdrawing he debates in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers, and daily in the public square with whoever is there. His distress turns into conversation.
elements.mainPoint: Paul’s distress at the city’s idols **drives him to speak**, in the synagogue and in the marketplace.

elements.question: What do the philosophers say about Paul in verse 18, and what message had he been proclaiming?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the two groups of philosophers.
elements.questionHint:
Find the two schools named.
Find two reactions to Paul.
Find what Luke says Paul was proclaiming.
elements.sampleAnswer: Some Epicurean and Stoic thinkers engage him. A few sneer at him as a ‘foolish babbler’, while others suppose he is promoting strange foreign deities. Luke notes that his actual subject was Jesus and the resurrection.
elements.mainPoint: Athens treats **Jesus and the resurrection** as odd imported ideas, and some dismiss Paul as a foolish babbler.

elements.question: Why do the Athenians bring Paul to the Areopagus in verses 19–21?
elements.questionHintFirst: Verse 21 explains the Athenian habit.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they ask Paul.
Find why they want to hear him.
Find how verse 21 describes how they spend their time.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Athenians take Paul to the Areopagus because they want to learn what this fresh teaching is, as it sounds strange to them. Luke explains that Athenians and visitors alike spent their free time on nothing but telling or hearing the latest idea. They are curious about novelty, which is not the same as seeking truth.
elements.mainPoint: The Athenians are **curious about what is new**, which is not the same as seeking the truth.

elements.passageText:
22So Paul stood before the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that you are very religious in all respects. 23For as I went around and observed closely your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: ‘To an unknown god.’ Therefore what you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you.

24The God who made the world and everything in it, who is Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by human hands, 25nor is he served by human hands, as if he needed anything, because he himself gives life and breath and everything to everyone. 26From one man he made every nation of the human race to inhabit the entire earth, determining their set times and the fixed limits of the places where they would live, 27so that they would search for God and perhaps grope around for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. 28For in him we live and move about and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’ 29So since we are God’s offspring, we should not think the deity is like gold or silver or stone, an image made by human skill and imagination.

30Therefore, although God has overlooked such times of ignorance, he now commands all people everywhere to repent, 31because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness, by a man whom he designated, having provided proof to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

32Now when they heard about the resurrection from the dead, some began to scoff, but others said, “We will hear you again about this.” 33So Paul left the Areopagus. 34But some people joined him and believed. Among them were Dionysius, who was a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

elements.question: What common ground does Paul find with the Athenians in verses 22–23, and what does he say about the altar ‘To an unknown god’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how Paul begins.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Paul says about their religion.
Find what he saw as he went around.
Find what he says about what they do not know.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul begins by saying he notices how religious they are in every way. Walking round, he found an altar labelled ‘To an unknown god’. He then announces that the one they worship unknowingly is the one he is making known to them.
elements.mainPoint: Paul **starts where they are**, with their altar to an unknown god, and makes that God known to them.

elements.question: What does Paul say about God as Creator in verses 24–26?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about what the Creator needs, and what he gives.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God made, and where he does not live.
Find what he does not need from us.
Find what he made from one man.
elements.sampleAnswer: The God who created the cosmos and all it holds rules heaven and earth, so he cannot be housed in shrines built by people. He needs nothing from human service, because he himself supplies life, breath and everything else. From a single man he produced every nation, fixing their eras and borders.
elements.mainPoint: Because **God is the Creator who made the world and gives life and breath to all**, he cannot be confined to a human-built sanctuary and is not dependent on our service.

elements.question: Why does God do this, according to verse 27, and what follows for how we think about God in verses 28–29?
elements.questionHintFirst: Find the purpose in verse 27, and then the conclusion in verse 29.
elements.questionHint:
Find why God did this.
Find how close God is.
Find what we should not think God is like.
elements.sampleAnswer: God’s aim was that people would look for him and perhaps feel their way towards him, although he is not far from any of us. In him we have our life, our movement and our being, and even their own poets call us his children. We must therefore not imagine God as like gold, silver or carved stone, an image shaped by human skill and invention.
elements.mainPoint: God is **near to us**, not far from any of us, and as his offspring we must not picture him as gold, silver or stone.

elements.question: What does Paul say God now commands in verse 30, and why does he give this command in verse 31?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the word ‘now’.
elements.questionHint:
Find what God has overlooked.
Find what he now commands.
Find the day, the judge and the proof.
elements.sampleAnswer: God has been patient with human ignorance in the past, but now he calls on everyone everywhere to repent. He has fixed a date on which he will judge the world fairly through a man he has appointed. He has given everyone assurance of this by bringing that man back from the dead.
elements.mainPoint: **Repentance is urgent for everyone**, because God has appointed a day to judge the world and has guaranteed it by raising Jesus.

elements.question: How do the Athenians respond in verses 32–34? Describe the different reactions.
elements.questionHintFirst: There are more than two reactions.
elements.questionHint:
Find those who scoff.
Find those who want to hear again.
Find those who believe, and who is named.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mention of rising from the dead made some of the listeners mock. Others said they wanted to hear more from him at another time. A few attached themselves to Paul and trusted, among them Dionysius from the Areopagus council and a woman called Damaris.
elements.mainPoint: The message meets **scoffing, curiosity and faith**: some mock, some want to hear again, and a few, such as Dionysius, believe.

elements.question: Paul was upset by the idols but still took the time to look closely at Athens. How do you tend to react to the culture around you, and what would it look like to engage as Paul did?
Paul begins with God as Creator and ends with the resurrection and judgement. If you had a few minutes with someone who knew nothing about the Bible, where would you begin?
Some scoffed, some wanted to hear more, and some believed. How do you cope with the different ways people respond when you share your faith?

elements.text: Paul meets Athens where it is, but he does not stay there. He speaks of the one Creator God who commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has appointed a day of judgement and given proof by raising Jesus from the dead. To read a fuller account of the journeys that led Paul here, tap Read more. In our last session we follow Paul to Rome.

Our final passage takes us to the end of Acts. Paul has reached Rome as a prisoner, and the story closes with him preaching in a rented house. Notice how Luke ends the book, and what that suggests about where the story goes next.

elements.question: What has stood out to you so far as you have followed the story of Acts?

elements.text: From Athens Paul goes to Corinth, where he stays for eighteen months with Priscilla and Aquila and is brought before the proconsul Gallio. In Ephesus, over about two years, the word spreads across the province of Asia until a riot is stirred up by the silversmiths. Paul revisits Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus at Troas, and at Miletus gives a moving farewell to the Ephesian elders. He sails to Jerusalem despite warnings of what awaits him. There he is seized in the temple, rescued by the Roman commander, and defends himself before the crowd and the council. Plots against his life lead to his transfer to Caesarea, where he is tried before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa. Appealing to Caesar, he sails for Rome, survives a violent storm and shipwreck on Malta, and finally reaches the city to the welcome of the believers.

elements.body: Before you begin, read Acts 28:1–16 in your own Bible to see how Paul reaches Rome. If you would like a fuller account of the eleven chapters before that, tap Read more at the end of this session.

elements.passageText:
17After three days Paul called the local Jewish leaders together.
