When they had assembled, he said to them, “Brothers, although I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors, from Jerusalem I was handed over as a prisoner to the Romans. 18When they had heard my case, they wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me. 19But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar—not that I had some charge to bring against my own people. 20So for this reason I have asked to see you and speak with you, for I am bound with this chain because of the hope of Israel.” 21They replied, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, nor have any of the brothers come from there and reported or said anything bad about you. 22But we would like to hear from you what you think, for regarding this sect we know that people everywhere speak against it.”

23They set a day to meet with him, and they came to him where he was staying in even greater numbers. From morning until evening he explained things to them, testifying about the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus from both the law of Moses and the prophets. 24Some were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.

25So they began to leave, unable to agree among themselves, after Paul made one last statement: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly to your ancestors through the prophet Isaiah 26when he said, ‘Go to this people and say, “You will keep on hearing, but will never understand, and you will keep on looking, but will never perceive. 27For the heart of this people has become dull, and their ears are hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they would not see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.”’ 28“Therefore be advised that this salvation from God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen!”

30Paul lived there two whole years in his own rented quarters and welcomed all who came to him, 31proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without restriction.

elements.question: How does Paul explain to the Jewish leaders in verses 17–20 why he is a prisoner in Rome?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what Paul says he has not done.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Paul says about his people and their customs.
Find what happened in Jerusalem, and what the Romans wanted.
Find why he appealed to Caesar, and why he is chained.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul tells the Jewish leaders he has committed no offence against his people or their ancestral customs, yet he was turned over from Jerusalem to the Romans. The Romans meant to free him, but because the Jews objected he had to appeal to Caesar. He explains that he wears this chain for the sake of Israel’s hope.
elements.mainPoint: Paul is **innocent**; he is in chains **because of the hope of Israel**, and appealed to Caesar only because he had to.

elements.question: How do the Jewish leaders reply in verses 21–22?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice what they have not heard, and what they have.
elements.questionHint:
Find what they say about letters and reports.
Find what they want from Paul.
Find what they know about this sect.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Jewish leaders reply that they have received no letters about Paul from Judea, and nobody has reported anything evil about him. They would like to hear his views directly. They do know, however, that this movement is denounced everywhere.
elements.mainPoint: The leaders have **no complaint against Paul**, no letters or bad reports, yet know that the movement is spoken against everywhere.

elements.question: What does Paul do in verse 23 when they come to him in greater numbers, and what is his message?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how long Paul speaks, and what he uses.
elements.questionHint:
Find how long Paul speaks.
Find the two things he testifies about.
Find the two parts of Scripture he uses.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul spends the whole day with them, from dawn until dusk, explaining and bearing witness to God’s kingdom. He tries to win them over about Jesus using both the Law of Moses and the prophets. His aim is to persuade them from Scriptures they already accept.
elements.mainPoint: Paul **argues from the Old Testament** that Jesus brings God’s kingdom, using both the Law and the Prophets.

elements.question: How do the listeners respond in verses 24–25, and what is the result?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the split.
elements.questionHint:
Find the two reactions.
Find what the group does next.
elements.sampleAnswer: Some of the listeners were won over by Paul’s words, while others would not trust. They were at odds with one another and started to depart. The same message therefore brings faith in some and rejection in others.
elements.mainPoint: The message **divides** its hearers: some are convinced, and others refuse to believe, so they disagree and begin to leave.

elements.question: What does Paul say that the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah in verses 25–27?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice who spoke through Isaiah.
elements.questionHint:
Find who Paul says spoke.
Find what the people hear and see.
Find what they fail to do.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the Holy Spirit rightly addressed their forefathers through the prophet Isaiah. They would go on listening yet never grasp, and go on looking yet never perceive. Their hearts have grown thick and their ears heavy, and they have shut their eyes, so that they would never turn and be healed.
elements.mainPoint: The Spirit foretold through Isaiah a people who **hear but never understand**, whose hearts have grown dull.

elements.question: What does Paul announce in verse 28?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice who receives the salvation.
elements.questionHint:
Find where the salvation has been sent.
Find what Paul says the Gentiles will do.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul announces that this saving message from God has been dispatched to the Gentiles. He adds that they will listen. Thus the good news is moving beyond Israel to the nations.
elements.mainPoint: God’s **salvation goes to the Gentiles**, and they will listen.

elements.question: How does Luke describe Paul’s situation in Rome in verse 30?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the length of time, and the welcome.
elements.questionHint:
Find how long Paul stayed, and where.
Find who he welcomed.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stayed in Rome for a full two years, living at his own expense in a hired house. He received everyone who visited him. No group was excluded from his hospitality.
elements.mainPoint: Paul’s rented house in Rome is **an open door**: for two whole years he welcomed all who came to him.

elements.question: What was Paul doing in Rome according to verse 31, and how do the last words of the book describe it?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the very last words of the book.
elements.questionHint:
Find what Paul proclaims and teaches.
Find the two phrases about how he did it.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul was proclaiming God’s kingdom and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. He did this with total confidence and with nothing to hinder him. The book closes not with Paul’s trial or death but with the gospel advancing freely from Rome.
elements.mainPoint: The gospel goes on **freely and boldly** from Rome, with nothing to hold back its preaching of the kingdom.

elements.question: Acts ends with the gospel unhindered but the story unfinished. What does it mean for you that the story continues today?
Paul kept welcoming everyone who came and kept proclaiming Jesus, even though he was confined. How can you keep witnessing within your own limits?
Looking back over the eight sessions, which passage has challenged or encouraged you most, and what one step will you take as a result?

elements.text: Acts ends with Paul in Rome, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without restriction. Luke leaves the story open because it is still going on. The same risen Lord who gave the mission in chapter 1 is still at work by his Spirit. To read a fuller account of the chapters leading up to Rome, tap Read more. You may want to read through the whole of Acts now that you have seen its shape.

footnotes.body: Theophilus means ‘friend of God’ or ‘one who loves God’. In his Gospel Luke calls him ‘most excellent’, which may suggest a person of standing.
Luke’s two volumes together make up roughly a quarter of the New Testament.

author.body:
Acts does not name its author, but it opens by addressing Theophilus and referring back to an earlier book about everything Jesus began to do and teach.[[fn:1]] Christians have always recognised that earlier book as the Gospel of Luke, so Acts is the second part of a single work in two volumes.[[fn:2]]

Luke was a companion of Paul. In some passages the narrative slips from ‘they’ into ‘we’, which suggests that the writer was present for part of the story.[[fn:3]] The book itself gives no date. It ends with Paul still preaching in Rome and does not tell us what happened at his trial, so many scholars think it was completed in the early 60s AD, though others date it later. Either way, it covers events from about AD 30 to about AD 60.

purpose.body:
Luke tells us his purpose at the start of his Gospel: he wants Theophilus to be sure of the things he has been taught (Luke 1:1–4). Acts continues that aim. It shows that the gospel is not a private sect but a message for the whole world. It shows that the Holy Spirit is the one who drives the mission forward. And it shows that God’s purposes cannot be stopped, whether by persecution, prison, storm or shipwreck.

It also tells readers who are not Jewish that they belong in the story. The God who made promises to Israel is now gathering people from every nation to himself through Jesus.

world.body:
Acts is set in the Roman Empire. Roman roads and sea routes made travel possible on a scale that had not been seen before, and Greek was understood almost everywhere. Jewish communities had settled in most major cities, and their synagogues gave the first missionaries a ready audience of Jews and of Gentiles who admired the Jewish faith. Roman law and Roman officials appear throughout the book, and Paul’s Roman citizenship becomes important in the later chapters.

The story moves through places that are now in Israel, Syria, Turkey, Greece and Italy. A map in your Bible, or one found online, will help you follow Paul’s travels.

shape.body:
Acts 1:8 gives Luke’s outline. Here is how the chapters fall within it.

StageChaptersWhat happens
Jerusalem1–7The ascension, Pentecost, the first church, opposition, Stephen
Judea and Samaria8–12Philip, the conversion of Saul, Cornelius, the church at Antioch
Paul’s journeys13–21Three journeys, and the council at Jerusalem in chapter 15
Paul the prisoner21–28Arrest, trials, the voyage and Rome

reading.body:
Acts is narrative. Luke records what happened, and he chooses and arranges events to teach. Some things in Acts happened once and were never meant to be repeated, such as the first coming of the Spirit at Pentecost and the special role of the apostles. Other things set a pattern for every generation, such as devotion to prayer, generous love for one another and bold witness.

A useful question to ask of any passage is: what is Luke showing us about God, about Jesus and about the gospel? A second is: what does the rest of the Bible say about the same thing?

spiritBaptism.header: A question Christians ask: baptised with the Spirit (1:5)
spiritBaptism.body:
Jesus tells the apostles that they will be baptised with the Holy Spirit within a few days. Christians understand this in three main ways. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians see Spirit baptism as a distinct experience given after conversion, which empowers for witness. Many Reformed and evangelical Christians see it as Christ’s one act of bringing his people into the Spirit’s life, so that every believer is baptised in the Spirit when they come to faith (compare 1 Corinthians 12:13), and Pentecost is the unique day on which this began for the whole church. A third group, including some respected Reformed teachers, holds that believers may later receive a deeper assurance or sealing by the Spirit, without making that a second stage everyone must pass through.

All three agree on what verse 8 says: the Spirit’s coming brings power to witness. All agree that believers should be filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).

This study takes the second view. Pentecost is a once-for-all event in the history of salvation, and every believer shares in what it brought. The later ‘Pentecost-like’ moments in Acts are best read in the same way, as steps in that history rather than patterns for each person’s experience. In Samaria (chapter 8) the gospel moves for the first time beyond Jerusalem and Judea, as Jesus said it would in verse 8. At Cornelius’s house (chapter 10) it reaches God-fearing Gentiles. In Ephesus (chapter 19) it catches up some disciples of John the Baptist, who had come to believe in Jesus to some degree but had been left behind by events. Those who hold other views are not asked to leave them behind, but this study does not build on them.

kingdomIsrael.header: A question Christians ask: the kingdom and Israel (1:6–7)
kingdomIsrael.body:
The apostles ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel. Jesus does not say the question is wrong, but he says the timing is not theirs to know, and he turns them towards their task. Christians read this in two main ways. Some, often called dispensational or premillennial, hold that the kingdom will be restored to national Israel in a future age, and that Jesus’ answer postpones this rather than denies it. Others, often called covenantal or amillennial, hold that the kingdom has already been restored in Jesus, who now reigns at God’s right hand (2:33–36), so that Israel’s hope is fulfilled in him and in the people gathered around him, and will be completed when he returns.

Both views take verse 7 seriously: no one can read the calendar. Both take verse 8 seriously: the task until Christ returns is witness.

This study leans to the second view. The kingdom has been inaugurated in Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation, and will be completed when he returns. It does not try to describe the end-times calendar, and it recognises that sincere Christians read the passage differently.

try.body: Read Acts 1:8 again. Then skim through Acts in your own Bible and note where Jerusalem, Samaria and Rome first appear. How does the book follow the plan Jesus gave?

chapters.title: Waiting, Pentecost and what led up to it

footnotes.body: Luke lists the people in the upper room in 1:13. Eleven of the Twelve are named, with Judas no longer among them.
Pentecost means ‘fiftieth’. The festival fell fifty days after Passover and is also called the Feast of Weeks.

waiting.body: The apostles return from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and gather in an upstairs room. Luke lists the eleven by name and adds that they were joined by several women, by Mary the mother of Jesus and by Jesus’ brothers.[[fn:1]] Luke records that they were all devoting themselves to prayer. They have been told to wait for the Father’s promise, and what they do while waiting is pray together.

matthias.body:
Peter stands up among about 120 believers and says that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture, and that the place he left must be filled. The replacement must be someone who has been with the group from John’s baptism until the ascension, and who can be a witness to Jesus’ resurrection. Two men are put forward, the group prays, lots are cast, and Matthias is added to the eleven.

The Twelve recall the twelve tribes of Israel, which suggests that Jesus is gathering a renewed people. This is the last time Acts records a decision made by casting lots. From the next chapter on, the Spirit has come and the church moves forward in a different way.

pentecost.body:
Pentecost was a Jewish harvest festival, and it drew pilgrims to Jerusalem from across the Mediterranean world.[[fn:2]] Luke tells us that a sound like a violent wind filled the house, that what looked like tongues of fire appeared and rested on each of them, and that all of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them.

The crowd gathered at the noise and was bewildered, because each person heard the believers speaking in his own language. The list of nations in verses 9–11 is long, and the message that people heard was about the wonders of God. Some readers see here a reversal of Babel, where languages divided the nations. Luke himself simply records the astonishment, the question ‘What does this mean?’ and the sneering of others who said they were drunk.

joel.body:
Peter stands with the Eleven and answers the charge of drunkenness: it is only nine in the morning. He then explains what is happening by quoting the prophet Joel, who foretold a time when God would pour out his Spirit on all kinds of people, young and old, men and women, and when everyone who calls on the name of the Lord would be saved.

Peter is saying that the last days have begun. The Spirit is not a private blessing for a few, but the gift of God’s age of salvation. Peter’s sermon in the next verses, which is the passage we study this session, shows who the Lord is on whose name people are to call.

repentBaptism.header: A question Christians ask: repentance, baptism and the Spirit (2:38)
repentBaptism.body:
Peter tells the crowd to repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of sins, and promises the gift of the Spirit. Three readings are common. Some traditions read this as teaching that forgiveness is given in baptism itself. Many Reformed and evangelical Christians read ‘for’ as meaning ‘with reference to’ or ‘on the basis of’, so that baptism is the outward sign and seal of the forgiveness that comes through repentance and faith. Others stress that ‘repent’ is addressed to the whole crowd and ‘be baptised’ to each person, and that repentance is the heart of the command.

Everyone agrees that Peter calls people to turn to Jesus, to be baptised in his name, and to expect forgiveness and the Spirit. Other passages in Acts also show forgiveness and the Spirit following faith (3:19; 10:43–44; 15:9).

This study takes the second view. Baptism is the sign and seal of what God gives to those who repent and believe, not the means by which forgiveness is earned or conferred. It is commanded, and not optional.

sharingGoods.header: A question Christians ask: sharing goods (2:44–45; 4:32–37)
sharingGoods.body:
The first believers held things in common and sold property to help those in need. Some Christians through history have taken this as a model for every church, with shared ownership as the ideal. Others observe that Luke presents the giving as voluntary (5:4 says the property was Ananias’s own to keep), as made in response to need (the verbs suggest sales as need arose), and as not repeated as a rule in the later chapters or in the letters. Still others see in it a principle: love is open-handed with those in need.

All agree that the passage shows believers who regarded their possessions as available for others, and that Luke holds this up as admirable.

This study treats the principle as binding and the particular form as not. Christians are to be generous with what they have, to meet real need and to count their possessions as God’s gift. They are not commanded to sell everything or to abolish private property.

try.body: Read Joel 2:28–32, then read Acts 2:17–21. What changes has Peter made, if any, and what does he add in the verses that follow?

chapters.title: The healing at the temple gate

footnotes.body: The ‘ninth hour’ was about three o’clock in the afternoon, one of the set times for prayer in the temple.

gate.body:
Peter and John are going up to the temple at the hour of prayer.[[fn:1]] At the temple gate called Beautiful sits a man who has been lame since birth and is carried there every day to beg. Peter tells him they have no silver or gold, but that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene he should walk. Peter takes him by the hand, and at once the man’s feet and ankles are strengthened. He leaps up, walks into the temple with them, and praises God.

Notice what the man receives. He asked for money and was given far more. Notice too that the miracle is done in Jesus’ name, which is exactly what the authorities will ask about in chapter 4.

crowd.body:
The people who had known the man as a beggar are filled with wonder, and they gather in Solomon’s Portico. Peter refuses any credit: this is not his own power or godliness, but the work of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who has glorified his servant Jesus. Peter reminds them that they handed Jesus over and rejected the Holy and Righteous One, but that God raised him from the dead and that he and John are witnesses. It is faith in Jesus’ name that has made this man strong.

Peter then says that the people acted in ignorance, as did their rulers, and that God was fulfilling what the prophets had foretold about a suffering Christ. He calls them to repent and turn to God, so that their sins may be wiped out and times of refreshing may come from the Lord. He reminds them of Moses’ promise of a prophet like himself, and tells them that they are heirs of the prophets and of the covenant, in which God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed. God raised up his servant and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each of them from wickedness.

pattern.body: Compare this sermon with Peter’s in chapter 2. Both begin with something that draws a crowd. Both point to Jesus as crucified and raised, and both end with a call to repent. And both are followed by the authorities’ reaction, which is what we study this session.

planAndResponsibility.header: A question Christians ask: God’s plan and human responsibility (4:27–28)
planAndResponsibility.body:
The believers’ prayer says that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel did what God’s power and plan had decided beforehand. In chapter 2 Peter says that those who killed Jesus acted by God’s plan and were still responsible for what they did (2:23). Christians have long thought about how these fit together. Many Reformed writers say that God ordains everything that happens, including evil acts, without being the author of evil and without removing the responsibility of those who do them. Others stress God’s foreknowledge: God knew what people would freely choose and worked it into his plan. Many simply say that Scripture holds both truths together and does not explain how.

All agree on what the believers do with this truth: it makes them confident rather than fearful, because God is in control even of those who oppose him.

This study takes a compatibilist position, the first view. God’s plan really includes these events, and the people who carried them out are fully responsible. It holds this as a mystery to be believed rather than solved, and does not argue against those who prefer the second view.

try.body: Read Acts 3:12–26 and list the names or titles Peter uses for Jesus. What does each tell you about who Jesus is?

footnotes.body: Barnabas’s name means ‘son of encouragement’, which Luke tells us in 4:36 was a nickname given by the apostles.
Gamaliel is described as a teacher of the law who was respected by all the people. His advice was to wait and see whether the movement was of God.

people.body:
These chapters introduce several people you will meet again.

PersonWhereWhy they matter
BarnabasJerusalem, 4:36–37Sells a field to help the needy; later vouches for Saul and travels with him
Ananias and SapphiraJerusalem, 5:1–11Pretend to give everything and lie to the Holy Spirit
GamalielJerusalem, 5:34–39A Pharisee on the council who urges caution towards the apostles
StephenJerusalem, 6:8–7:60Full of grace and the Spirit; the first martyr in Acts
PhilipSamaria and the Gaza road, 8:4–40Takes the gospel to Samaritans and to an Ethiopian official
SimonSamaria, 8:9–24A sorcerer who believes, but misunderstands the Spirit as something to buy

generosity.body:
Luke pauses to describe the church again: they were of one heart and soul, no one claimed that his possessions were his own, and those who owned land or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles, who distributed them as there was need. Barnabas is the example Luke names.[[fn:1]]

Ananias and Sapphira sell a piece of property, keep back part of the money and bring the rest as though it were the whole. Peter tells Ananias that he has lied to the Holy Spirit, and he falls down dead; Sapphira, when questioned, repeats the lie and meets the same fate. Great fear comes on the whole church. Notice that the sin was not in keeping some of the money, which was theirs to keep, but in pretending to give it all.

opposition.header: The apostles before the council again (5:12–42)
opposition.body:
Signs and wonders continue, the sick are brought out into the streets, and crowds come from the towns around Jerusalem. The high priest and the Sadducees arrest the apostles and put them in the public jail, but an angel opens the doors during the night and sends them back to the temple to teach. When they are brought before the council, Peter repeats what he said in chapter 4: we must obey God rather than men.

The council wants to kill them, but Gamaliel urges them to leave the apostles alone.[[fn:2]] The apostles are flogged and warned again, and they leave rejoicing that they have been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name. Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they go on teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.

seven.body: As the church grows, Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve ask the church to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to oversee this work, so that the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. All seven have Greek names. The church agrees, and Luke notes that the word of God continued to spread and that many priests became obedient to the faith.

stephen.body:
Stephen is full of grace and power and does great wonders among the people. When some from the synagogues cannot win the argument, they stir up the people and bring false witnesses before the council, charging him with speaking against the temple and the law. His long speech in chapter 7 retells Israel’s history, showing again and again how God’s people resisted the leaders and messengers God sent, and ends by accusing his hearers of doing the same to the Righteous One.

The council is furious. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, sees heaven open and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. They drag him out of the city and stone him, and as he dies he prays for Jesus to receive his spirit and asks that this sin not be held against his killers. A young man named Saul stands by, approving.

scattered.body:
A great persecution breaks out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles are scattered through Judea and Samaria. Saul begins to ravage the church, going from house to house. But those who are scattered go about preaching the word. Philip goes to Samaria and proclaims the Christ there, with signs and great joy in the city. When the apostles hear that Samaria has received the word of God, they send Peter and John, and the Holy Spirit is given.

Philip is then sent to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he meets an Ethiopian official reading the prophet Isaiah. Beginning from that Scripture, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus. The official believes and is baptised, and goes on his way rejoicing. The gospel has now crossed into Samaria and reached an African court official, moving outwards along the lines of Jesus’ words in 1:8.

conversionOrCall.header: A question Christians ask: conversion or calling? (9:1–22)
conversionOrCall.body:
Two questions arise from Saul’s encounter with Jesus. First, was it a conversion or a call? Some scholars say it was only a call, because Paul saw himself as remaining within the faith of Israel. Others say it was a conversion, because he turned from persecuting Jesus to trusting him as Lord. Most evangelicals say it was both. Second, when did Saul receive the Spirit: on the road, or through Ananias (verse 17)? Some think on the road, some through Ananias, and others that Luke does not tell us and does not intend us to build a pattern.

All agree that Jesus took the initiative, that Saul answered, and that his life was changed from that day.

This study treats it as both: Saul’s turning to Jesus as Lord was a true conversion, and the same encounter was his call to be an apostle. It does not build a pattern from the order of events with Ananias, since Luke does not either. Paul himself later says that God was pleased to reveal his Son in him (Galatians 1:15–16), which fits the view that salvation begins with God.

footnotes.body: Caesarea was built by Herod the Great and was the Roman administrative centre of Judea.
Peter’s words about animals that were clean or unclean refer to the food laws of the Old Testament. Jews who kept those laws would not normally eat with people who did not.

escape.body: After a number of days the Jews in Damascus plot to kill Saul, and his disciples help him escape by lowering him over the city wall in a basket. In Jerusalem the believers are afraid of him, until Barnabas takes him to the apostles and tells how Saul had seen the Lord and preached boldly in Damascus. Saul then speaks boldly in Jerusalem too, until some Greek-speaking Jews try to kill him and the brothers send him off to Tarsus. Luke then notes that the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace and was built up, and that it grew as it lived in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

lydda.body: Peter travels about the country and comes to Lydda, where he heals Aeneas, who has been paralysed and bedridden for eight years. In the coastal town of Joppa, a disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas in Greek) dies after a life full of good deeds and acts of charity. The believers send for Peter. He kneels and prays and tells her to get up, and she opens her eyes. The news spreads through Joppa and many believe in the Lord. Peter stays on for some time with a tanner named Simon.

cornelius.body: In Caesarea there lives a centurion named Cornelius, a man who is devout and God-fearing along with his whole household.[[fn:1]] He gives generously to those in need and prays to God regularly. At about three in the afternoon he has a vision in which an angel tells him that his prayers and gifts have come up as a memorial before God, and that he should send men to Joppa to bring back a man named Simon Peter. Cornelius obeys at once.

vision.body:
While the messengers are approaching Joppa, Peter goes up on the roof to pray and becomes hungry. He sees heaven opened and something like a large sheet being let down, containing all kinds of animals, reptiles and birds. A voice tells him to get up, kill and eat. Peter refuses, saying that he has never eaten anything impure or unclean. The voice replies that he must not call impure what God has made clean. This happens three times.[[fn:2]]

While Peter is still thinking about the vision, the Spirit tells him that three men are looking for him and that he should go with them without hesitation. Peter welcomes the men and invites them to stay the night.

meeting.body: The next day Peter sets out with some of the believers from Joppa. Cornelius has gathered his relatives and close friends, and when Peter arrives he falls at Peter’s feet. Peter lifts him up and says he is only a man. Peter then says that it is against Jewish custom for a Jew to visit or associate with a Gentile, but that God has shown him that he should call no one impure or unclean. When he asks why he has been sent for, Cornelius tells of the angel and says that they are all gathered in God’s presence to hear everything the Lord has commanded Peter to say. This is where our passage begins.

why.body: Luke gives this story a great deal of space, and he repeats it in the next chapter when Peter explains himself to the church in Jerusalem. It is the turning point of Acts. The vision about food, the invitation from a Gentile and the gift of the Spirit all point in one direction: the gospel is for every nation, and the church must learn what that means. That question will come to a head in chapter 15.

fearsGod.header: A question Christians ask: ‘fears him and does what is right’ (10:35)
fearsGod.body:
Peter says that in every nation the one who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him. Some read this as saying that sincere people of any religion are accepted by God. Others read it as saying that God does not favour one nation over another, and that people like Cornelius, who are seeking him, are the people who will hear the gospel and respond. Cornelius was devout and generous, but chapter 11 says that the angel told him to send for Peter so that he and his household might be saved (11:14), and Peter’s own message ends by saying that forgiveness comes through Jesus’ name (10:43).

All agree that the verse is about God’s impartiality, and not about earning salvation.

This study takes the second view. The verse is about nationality and background, and does not describe a different way of salvation. Cornelius needed Peter’s message, and the Spirit’s coming and baptism followed his faith.

spiritTongues.header: A question Christians ask: the Spirit and tongues (10:44–46)
spiritTongues.body:
The Spirit falls on the Gentiles while Peter is still speaking, and they are heard speaking in tongues and praising God. Luke describes the Spirit’s coming in different orders. In Jerusalem it follows baptism (2:38). In Samaria it follows baptism and the apostles’ visit (8:14–17). Here it comes before baptism. In Ephesus it follows baptism and Paul’s laying on of hands (19:1–7). This variety is one reason the study reads these events as stages in the spread of the gospel (see the Go Deeper chapter for session 1), not as a formula for individual experience. All agree that this event confirmed that Gentiles are welcomed on the same footing as Jewish believers (11:15–17).

Christians differ over what the tongues themselves were, and whether they continue today. There are several main views.

  • Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians hold that tongues continues as a gift, often as the first sign of being baptised in the Spirit, and that it may be a prayer language given by the Spirit as well as unlearned human languages.
  • Many Christians who are not Pentecostal agree that the gifts continue, but do not treat tongues as a required sign, and see it as one gift among many.
  • Cessationists hold that miraculous gifts, including tongues, belonged to the apostolic age and have ceased, and that tongues in Acts and 1 Corinthians were real foreign languages.
  • A further view holds that tongues in the New Testament always means real human languages, as many early Christian writers and the Reformers understood it, but that this need not always be a miracle of unlearned speech. At Pentecost the speakers were Galilean Jews who spoke languages they had not learned, which was plainly miraculous. At Cornelius’s house the speakers were Gentiles, and the surprise is to hear them praising Israel’s God aloud in languages of the nations, just as at Pentecost. On this view the point in each case is that God is praised in many languages, reversing Babel, whether or not the speakers had learned the language in the ordinary way. Those who find private non-verbal prayer helpful may see it as a form of the Spirit’s help when words fail (Romans 8:26), without equating it with the gift described in Acts.

The author of this study finds the last view persuasive, and offers it as one option among several. This study does not ask anyone to adopt it, and takes no side on whether miraculous gifts continue. It holds that every believer receives the Spirit when they believe (Romans 8:9), and that no one needs a special sign to be sure of this.

try.body: Read Acts 10:9–16 and then Acts 10:28. How does Peter apply the vision? What has the vision about food to do with the question of who may be welcomed?

footnotes.body: Luke tells us in 11:26 that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. The name seems to have been given by outsiders.
Saul is first called Paul in 13:9. Luke gives no explanation. Saul was his Hebrew name, and Paul was a Roman name he would have had as a Roman citizen.

peter.body: News that Gentiles have received the word of God reaches the apostles and believers in Judea, and when Peter returns to Jerusalem some of the circumcised believers criticise him for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter explains the whole sequence in order: his vision, the Spirit’s instruction to go, the six brothers who came with him, and what happened as he began to speak. He ends by asking who he was to stand in God’s way. The criticism falls silent, and they praise God, saying that God has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles.

antioch.body:
Those scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death travel as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, at first speaking the word only to Jews. But some men from Cyprus and Cyrene begin to speak to Greeks in Antioch, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus, and a great number believe. The church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who sees the grace of God at work and encourages them all. He then goes to Tarsus to find Saul, and the two teach a large group for a year. It is at Antioch that the disciples are first called Christians.[[fn:1]]

When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, the disciples in Antioch decide to send help to the believers in Judea, each according to his ability, and they send it by Barnabas and Saul.

herod.body:
King Herod Agrippa begins to persecute the church. He has James, the brother of John, killed with the sword, and when he sees that this pleases the Jews, he arrests Peter and puts him in prison, guarded by four squads of soldiers. The church prays earnestly for him. The night before his trial, an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off and he walks out past the guards. At the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, a servant girl named Rhoda recognises his voice, but the praying believers cannot believe it is him until they see him.

Herod’s end is abrupt. After accepting praise from a crowd as though he were a god, he is struck down by an angel of the Lord because he did not give glory to God. Luke concludes that the word of God continued to grow and to multiply.

commission.body: The church at Antioch has prophets and teachers from several backgrounds, including Barnabas and Saul. While they are worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has called them. After more fasting and prayer, the church lays hands on them and sends them off. It is the Spirit who sends them, and the church who releases them.

journey.header: The first journey at a glance (13:4–14:28)
journey.body:
Barnabas and Saul (who is called Paul from this point on)[[fn:2]], together with John Mark, sail first to Cyprus and then cross to the mainland of what is now southern Turkey. This table sets out the main stops.

PlaceWhat happenedResponse
Cyprus (13:4–12)Paul confronts a sorcerer; the proconsul Sergius Paulus listens to the wordThe proconsul believes
Pisidian Antioch (13:13–52)Paul preaches in the synagogue; the next Sabbath almost the whole city gathersMany Gentiles believe; some Jews stir up persecution
Iconium (14:1–7)Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue for some timeMany believe; the city is divided; a plot to stone them
Lystra (14:8–20)Paul heals a man lame from birth; the crowds take them for godsPaul is stoned and left for dead, but gets up and goes on
Derbe (14:20–21)They preach the good newsThey make many disciples

Paul and Barnabas then retrace their steps, strengthening the new churches and appointing elders in each, before returning to Antioch and reporting how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

amosQuotation.header: A question Christians ask: James and the rebuilt tent (15:16–18)
amosQuotation.body:
James quotes the prophet Amos about God rebuilding David’s fallen tent so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord. Some Christians, often dispensational, read ‘after this I will return’ as pointing to a future return of Christ after the church age, followed by the restoration of David’s kingdom for Israel and the blessing of the Gentiles. Others read the promise as already fulfilled: the risen and enthroned Son of David is the rebuilt tent, and Gentiles coming to Christ is the fruit. James does not say how and when the quotation will be completed. He says that it agrees with what Peter has described.

All agree on the point James draws: Gentiles may come to God without becoming Jews.

This study takes the second view. The promise to David is being fulfilled in Jesus now, and the inclusion of the Gentiles is part of it. It notes that others read the order differently.

fourRequirements.header: A question Christians ask: the four requirements (15:20)
fourRequirements.body:
James proposes that Gentile believers be asked to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled and from blood. Some have taken these as permanent rules for all Christians. Others see them as a temporary measure so that Jewish and Gentile believers could eat together in mixed churches, noting that Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love (1 Corinthians 8–10; Romans 14). Others read the list as a summary of moral concerns: idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed.

There is another suggestion, which the author of this study tentatively holds. These four were picked because they were the things most likely to divide Jewish Christians from Gentile Christians, so that part of the purpose was to make unity easier. Each was a pressure point at the table and in the life of a shared church. The council settles that Gentiles are saved by grace without the law, and then asks them to avoid the practices that Jewish believers would find hardest to bear.

All agree that the decision protects the gospel: nothing is added to grace. On this view the food rules were a loving and practical measure for that time, and are not to be imposed today. Idolatry and sexual immorality are always forbidden, and the principle of caring for one another’s consciences continues.

try.body: Read Acts 14:8–18, where the crowds at Lystra mistake Paul and Barnabas for gods. What does Paul say in reply about who God is? Compare this with what he says in Athens in the next session.

footnotes.body: Luke tells us in 16:3 that Paul had Timothy circumcised ‘because of the Jews who were in those places’. Timothy’s mother was Jewish and his father Greek. Paul’s refusal to circumcise Titus in Galatians 2 and his willingness here concern different circumstances.
The ‘we’ in 16:10 is the first of the passages where Luke writes as though he were present. It begins at Troas and continues in Philippi.
Roman citizens could not lawfully be beaten and jailed without a trial. The magistrates’ alarm in 16:38 shows how seriously they took this.

letter.body: The council sends Judas Barsabbas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas, carrying a letter to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. The letter says that the men who had troubled them had gone out without authority, and that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to the council not to place a greater burden on them than a few necessary things. When the letter is read at Antioch, the church rejoices at its encouragement. Judas and Silas strengthen the believers with many words.

split.body: Paul suggests going back to visit the churches of the first journey. Barnabas wants to take John Mark again, but Paul does not want to take someone who had left them earlier. The disagreement is so sharp that they separate. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chooses Silas and goes through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Luke does not tell us who was right, but notes that Paul was commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord.

timothy.body: At Lystra, Paul meets a disciple named Timothy, well spoken of by the believers there. Paul wants him to come along and has him circumcised, because of the Jews in that area who knew that his father was Greek.[[fn:1]] As they travel from town to town, they hand on the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches are strengthened in the faith and grow daily.

macedonia.body: The Spirit keeps Paul’s group from speaking the word in the province of Asia and does not allow them to enter Bithynia. They pass through Mysia and come down to Troas. There Paul has a vision in the night of a man of Macedonia pleading with him to come over and help them. Luke notes that immediately they set out, concluding that God had called them to preach the good news there. At this point the narrative changes from ‘they’ to ‘we’.[[fn:2]]

philippi.body:
On the Sabbath the missionaries go outside the city to a place of prayer and speak to the women gathered there. One of them, Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who worshipped God, listens, and Luke says that the Lord opened her heart to respond. She and her household are baptised. Paul then frees a slave girl from a spirit that made money for her owners, and the owners drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed.

At midnight, as Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the prison doors. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and he and his household are baptised that night. In the morning Paul reveals that they are Roman citizens, and the magistrates come and apologise.[[fn:3]]

thessalonica.body: In Thessalonica Paul goes into the synagogue on three Sabbaths and reasons with the Jews from the Scriptures, explaining that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus is the Christ. Some are persuaded, including a large number of God-fearing Greeks and several prominent women. Other Jews become jealous, gather a mob and attack the house of Jason, where the missionaries had been staying. When they cannot find Paul and Silas, they drag Jason and some believers before the city officials, charging that these men are acting against Caesar’s decrees by saying that there is another king, Jesus.

berea.body: The believers send Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. Luke says that the Jews there were more noble than those in Thessalonica, receiving the message with eagerness and examining the Scriptures daily to see whether what Paul said was true. Many believe, including prominent Greek women and men. But Jews from Thessalonica come and stir up the crowds, and the believers send Paul to the coast while Silas and Timothy stay behind. Those who escort Paul take him all the way to Athens.

whatAthensKnew.header: A question Christians ask: what people know of God (17:26–31)
whatAthensKnew.body:
Paul tells the Athenians that God made everyone to seek him, that he is not far from each of us, that he has overlooked times of ignorance, and that he now commands all people to repent. Christians differ on what this shows. Some say that Paul finds common ground in what people can know of God from creation, and builds on it. Others say that Paul begins from the God of Scripture and treats the Athenians’ ideas as something to be challenged, not built on. Some read ‘overlooked ignorance’ as meaning that ignorance is a kind of excuse until the message arrives. Others say it means God’s patience in the face of guilt (compare Romans 1:18–21).

All agree that Paul does not stop at common ground: he ends with repentance, a day of judgement and the resurrection.

This study holds that people know something of God but suppress it, that their ignorance is not innocent, and that God’s patience is an opportunity to repent rather than approval. It does not claim that Paul’s method is the only way to speak with unbelievers.

try.body: Read Acts 17:11 and think about how the Bereans listened to Paul. How do you check what you hear taught against the Scriptures?

footnotes.body: Gallio’s time as proconsul of Achaia can be dated from an inscription found at Delphi, and this gives a fixed point for dating Paul’s stay in Corinth, around AD 51 or 52.
The Artemis of Ephesus was worshipped in a vast temple which was counted among the wonders of the ancient world. Making silver shrines of the goddess was a thriving trade.
Luke gives the number as 276 people on board in 27:37, and says all of them reached land safely.

corinth.body: In Corinth Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple who had recently left Rome, and works with them as a tentmaker. He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath. When the Jews oppose him, he turns to the Gentiles, and Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes together with his household. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid, because he has many people in the city, and Paul stays for a year and a half. The Jews bring him before the proconsul Gallio, who refuses to judge a dispute about their law.[[fn:1]] Paul then sails back to Syria, visiting Ephesus on the way, and later returns to the churches of Galatia and Phrygia.

ephesus.body:
Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria who knew only the baptism of John, is taken aside by Priscilla and Aquila, who explain the way of God more accurately to him. At Ephesus Paul finds some disciples who have not heard of the Holy Spirit; when he lays hands on them after baptism in the name of Jesus, the Spirit comes. For two years he reasons daily in the hall of Tyrannus, so that all the Jews and Greeks living in Asia hear the word of the Lord. God does extraordinary miracles through Paul, and many who had practised magic burn their books.

The silversmith Demetrius stirs up a riot because the spread of the gospel is damaging the trade in silver shrines of Artemis.[[fn:2]] The crowd rushes into the theatre shouting, and the city clerk eventually calms them and sends them home.

miletus.body: Paul revisits Macedonia and Greece. At Troas, a young man named Eutychus falls from a window while Paul is preaching late into the night, and Paul raises him. At Miletus, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to meet him and gives his farewell. He reminds them how he served among them, warns them of false teachers who will arise even from within, and charges them to shepherd the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. They weep, embrace him and accompany him to the ship.

jerusalem.body:
Though disciples and the prophet Agabus warn him of what awaits him, Paul goes up to Jerusalem. Jews from Asia see him in the temple and stir up the crowd, who drag him out and try to kill him. The Roman commander rescues him and allows him to speak to the crowd from the steps. Paul tells his story, but the crowd erupts when he speaks of being sent to the Gentiles. As he is about to be flogged, Paul reveals that he is a Roman citizen.

The next day Paul speaks to the council and, knowing that it is made up of both Sadducees and Pharisees, calls out that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection. The assembly divides. The Lord stands beside Paul that night and tells him to take courage, for he must testify in Rome too. A plot of more than forty men to ambush him is discovered by Paul’s nephew, and the commander sends Paul under heavy guard to Caesarea.

caesarea.body:
In Caesarea Paul is heard in turn by three rulers.

RulerWhat happenedOutcome
Felix (ch. 24)Paul answers the charges of the high priest and the lawyer Tertullus; Felix and his wife listen to him speak about faith in ChristFelix keeps Paul in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe
Festus (ch. 25)Festus, the new governor, proposes to hear the case in JerusalemPaul appeals to Caesar
King Agrippa (ch. 26)Paul tells the story of his conversion and his callingAgrippa remarks that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed

In each hearing Paul uses the opportunity to testify about Jesus and about the hope of Israel, and in each the authorities find nothing in him deserving death.

voyage.body:
Paul sails for Rome in the custody of a centurion named Julius. After they leave Crete, a fierce storm drives the ship for days, and the crew give up hope of being saved. But an angel tells Paul that God has granted him the lives of all those sailing with him, and that he must stand before Caesar. After fourteen days the ship runs aground and breaks up, but everyone gets safely to shore.[[fn:3]]

On Malta, Paul is bitten by a snake and shakes it off without harm, and he heals the father of the chief official, Publius, and others on the island. Three months later they sail on, and at last reach Italy. Believers from Rome come out to meet Paul, and he thanks God and takes courage. Rome is where our passage begins.

next.body: If this study has whetted your appetite, the best next step is to read Acts through in one or two sittings. You will now recognise the big movements of the story and the places where you have paused. You might then read some of Paul’s letters alongside Acts. Many Christians connect several of his letters with the period of his imprisonment, and reading them with Acts in mind brings both to life.

hardeningAndIsrael.header: A question Christians ask: hardening and the future of Israel (28:25–28)
hardeningAndIsrael.body:
Paul quotes Isaiah about people who hear and never understand. Christians differ on two questions. First, who does the hardening? Many Reformed writers say that God hardens as a judgement, and that the people harden themselves. Others stress the people’s own refusal. Second, what does the passage mean for the Jewish people? Some say that the gospel has now moved from Israel to the Gentiles and that the church is the true Israel. Others, looking to Romans 9–11, say that Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary, and that many Jews will come to Christ. Some also expect a future turning of the nation.

All agree that the verses explain why many did not believe, and that the salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. All agree that Paul went on welcoming all who came to him (verse 30), which would include Jews.

This study holds that the hardening is both God’s judgement and the people’s own doing, in line with the compatibilist view taken in session 3. It holds that Acts 28 is not a final closing of the door on the Jewish people: the gospel remains for the Jew as well as the Gentile. It does not commit to a view on the end-times future of Israel.

try.body: Turn back to Acts 1:8 and read it once more. Which parts of the verse can you now trace through the book? What stage of the story do you think we are in today?

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Notes for group leaders
intro: These notes are for people who lead a group through Introducing Acts. They are part of the study file, so anyone who switches the page on can read them.

Each session is designed to be worked through beforehand by each member, on their own, and then discussed together. Members who have not had time to prepare can still take part: the passage opens in a pop-up from any question, and the questions are short.

A session works well in about an hour, though you can stretch it. Each set of notes gives the aim of the session, a suggested flow, and things to watch for. Where Christians who love the Bible equally differ on a point in the passage, the notes say so. You do not need to settle these differences; keep returning to what the passage says.

Because this is an overview, each session skips some chapters. The short summary at the start of each session and the Go Deeper section at the end fill in the gaps. Encourage members who want the full story to read the skipped chapters in their own Bibles.

You will find the study works best when you ask people to share what they wrote, and then ask ‘What makes you say that?’ rather than supplying answers. The sample answers inside the app are there to help individuals check their own work, not to be read out.

aim.body: To introduce the book of Acts, its main idea (the risen Jesus continuing his work through his witnesses by the Spirit) and the way this study works. Keep the focus on what the passage says. Newcomers need to feel that Acts is a story they can follow.

flow.body:
• Welcome, and a few words on how the study works (5 minutes).
  • The opening question: what do members already know about Acts? (10 minutes).
  • Work through the passage questions, letting members share what they wrote (30 minutes).
  • One or two of the reflection questions, then prayer (15 minutes).

Adjust the timings to suit your group.

differ.body:
Three verses in this passage are understood in different ways by Christians who love the Bible equally. Verse 5 speaks of being baptised with the Holy Spirit, and people differ about how this relates to conversion and to later experience. Verse 6 raises the question of the kingdom and Israel, and people differ about what Jesus’ answer implies for the future. Verse 11 promises Jesus’ return, and people differ over details of how the end will unfold.

You do not need to settle these. Ask ‘What does the passage say?’ and return to Jesus’ own focus in verse 8.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: Members who are new to the Bible may find the opening session quiet. Encourage short answers. Members who know Acts well may want to jump ahead to Pentecost; remind them that we reach it next time.

aim.body: To see how the first Christian sermon centres on Jesus’ death and resurrection, and to notice the shape of the community that formed in response. Keep returning to ‘What does the passage say?’

flow.body:
• The opening question about who Jesus is (10 minutes).
  • The sermon, verses 22–36, with attention to Peter’s argument from David (25 minutes).
  • The response and the community, verses 37–47 (20 minutes).
  • A reflection question and prayer (10 minutes).

differ.body:
Two points here are understood differently by Christians who love the Bible equally. In verse 38, people differ over how repentance, baptism, forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit fit together. In verses 44–45, people differ over whether the sharing of goods is a pattern for every church or a particular response by that community.

Keep to the text: ask what Peter tells them to do and what he promises, and what the believers did. Avoid pressing members to commit to one reading.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: The Pentecost events in verses 1–13 are in the catch-up section, and members may ask about tongues. Acknowledge the question, note that the passage for this session begins with Peter’s sermon, and say that we will meet the gift of the Spirit again in session 5.

aim.body: To see how the apostles respond to opposition: with a clear testimony about Jesus, with obedience to God above human authority, and with prayer for courage.

flow.body:
• The opening question about keeping quiet under pressure (10 minutes).
  • The trial before the council, verses 1–22 (25 minutes).
  • The prayer of the church, verses 23–31 (15 minutes).
  • Reflection and prayer (15 minutes).

differ.body:
Verses 27–28 say that those who put Jesus to death did what God’s power and plan had decided beforehand. Christians have long thought about how God’s plan and human responsibility fit together. You do not need to resolve this. Ask what the believers say about God here, and how they respond to it in prayer.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: Some members may live with real pressure or danger for their faith, and others may be tempted to treat the passage as a distant story. Give space for people to say how this feels where they live, and pray for those who suffer for the name of Jesus.

aim.body: To see Jesus take the initiative with an opponent of the church, and to notice how God uses ordinary believers like Ananias. Keep the focus on what the passage says about Jesus’ action and Saul’s response.

flow.body:
• The opening question about unlikely converts (10 minutes).
  • The encounter on the road, verses 1–9 (20 minutes).
  • Ananias and Saul, verses 10–22 (25 minutes).
  • Reflection and prayer for those far from God (10 minutes).

differ.body:
Christians differ over how to describe what happened to Saul: whether his experience is best called a conversion, a calling or both, and how far it is a pattern for others. Christians also differ over how the Spirit’s filling in verse 17 relates to the Spirit’s work in a person’s conversion.

Both are good questions. For this session, ask what Jesus says and does, and what Saul and Ananias do in response.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: Members may think of a particular person for whom they have given up hope. Allow time for this, and gently point out that Saul’s story starts with Jesus, not with Saul’s change of heart. End with prayer for those who come to mind.

aim.body: To see that the gospel is for every nation, that Jesus is Lord of all, and that God himself confirms this by giving the Spirit to Gentiles. Keep the focus on Peter’s message about Jesus and on what God does.

flow.body:
• The opening question about who might feel unwelcome (10 minutes).
  • Peter’s message, verses 34–43 (25 minutes).
  • The Spirit falls, verses 44–48, and the comparison question (15 minutes).
  • Reflection and prayer (15 minutes).

differ.body:
Two matters here are understood differently by Christians who love the Bible equally. The first is how to read verse 35: some read it as saying that God welcomes anyone who sincerely seeks him, and others read it alongside verse 43, which says that forgiveness comes through believing in Jesus. The second is how the Spirit’s coming and speaking in tongues in verses 44–46 relate to what happened at Pentecost and to the church today.

You do not need to resolve either. Ask what Peter says in verse 43, and what God does in verses 44–46, and let the group notice how the two halves belong together.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: The opening question is about welcome. Members may name people who they find hard to welcome. Listen kindly, and do not rush to correct. Make sure the group sees that the passage is about God’s welcome before it is about ours.

aim.body: To see that the gospel of grace is for Jews and Gentiles alike, and to learn from the way the church handles a serious disagreement. Keep the focus on what the passage says about how people are saved.

flow.body:
• The opening question about disagreement (10 minutes).
  • The question is raised, verses 1–11 (25 minutes).
  • The council’s decision, verses 12–21 (20 minutes).
  • Reflection and prayer (10 minutes).

differ.body:
Christians who love the Bible equally differ on two matters here. The first is how James’s quotation from the prophet Amos in verses 16–18 relates to Israel, the church and the future. The second is how the four requirements in verse 20 apply today.

You do not need to settle either. Ask what James says the quotation shows, and what the council asks of the Gentile believers and why.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: The passage is about the gospel itself, so the group may find it easy to agree and hard to apply. Press gently on the reflection questions: where do we add to grace? Be ready for members to bring up real disagreements in your own church, and keep the conversation kind and focused on what the passage says.

aim.body: To see how Paul speaks about God, creation, repentance and the resurrection to an audience with no knowledge of the Bible, and to notice the mixed response. Keep the focus on what Paul says and how people respond.

flow.body:
• The opening question: how would you explain who God is? (10 minutes).
  • Paul in the city, verses 16–21 (15 minutes).
  • Paul’s speech, verses 22–31 (25 minutes).
  • The response, verses 32–34, then reflection and prayer (15 minutes).

differ.body:
Christians who love the Bible equally differ on how to understand parts of this speech. One question is how far people can know God from creation, and how Paul’s words about people searching for God in verse 27 fit with his words about ignorance and repentance in verses 29–30. Another is how Paul’s approach here should shape the way we explain the gospel today.

You do not need to resolve these. Ask what Paul says about God, about humanity and about Jesus, and what he asks people to do.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: The group may be tempted to spend the whole time debating how to do evangelism well. Keep it grounded in the passage first, and then use the reflection questions to let people share real experiences, including fears. Encourage members to take one practical step this week.

aim.body: To see how Acts ends: with Paul still proclaiming Jesus, and the gospel moving beyond Israel to the nations. This is also the chance to look back over the whole study and to think about what comes next.

flow.body:
• The opening question: what has stood out so far? (10 minutes).
  • Paul and the Jewish leaders, verses 17–28 (25 minutes).
  • The ending, verses 30–31 (10 minutes).
  • Reflection, looking back over the eight sessions, and prayer (20 minutes).

verse.body: Some members may notice that the verses jump from 28 to 30. Verse 29 is not included in the NET Bible, because it is missing from the earliest manuscripts. Some older English translations include it. It does not affect the meaning of the passage.

differ.body:
Christians who love the Bible equally differ over how to understand Paul’s quotation from Isaiah in verses 26–27 and his announcement in verse 28. Some emphasise God’s judicial hardening of the unbelieving, and others emphasise the people’s own refusal to listen. Christians also differ over what the passage implies for the future of Israel, a question Paul takes up at length in Romans 9–11.

You do not need to settle this. Ask what Paul says the Spirit said through Isaiah, and what Paul concludes.

The Go Deeper section for this session sets out the main views and says where this study stands. Read it before the session if you can, but keep the group’s discussion on what the passage says.

watch.body: This is the last session, so leave time to look back. You may want to ask members what they have learned, what has surprised them, and whether they would like to continue with another study, such as reading through the whole of Acts together or a study of one of the Gospels.

publisher.name: BeaconLight
paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
BeaconLight is a member of the Evangelical Alliance and Global Connections, and is a registered charity in England and Wales (Charity No. 1047046).
